neighbours.secrets: Cyra, Erebos's patron, curses whoever comes into the valley meaning the covenant harm.

neighbours.name: The Spring of Larissa
neighbours.summary: The spring whose kindly nymph gave Larissa its name. She is still glimpsed now and then and the townsfolk revere her as a saint; she and the horse of the Thessalian plain are the city's two old emblems. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Meteora
neighbours.summary:
'Hanging in the heavens': a forest of huge sandstone pillars, some over a thousand feet tall, near the north-west edge of the Thessalian plain where the Salambria leaves the Pindos. On top, especially when mist fills the plain, one feels marooned on a little island near Heaven. The skete of Doupiani lives here, and most pillars have Divine auras from 3 to 6, each named for the mystic experience found on it (the Pillar of Dreams, of Solitude and so on).

Giant Divine eagles nest among the pillars: a devout, humble hermit who falls may be caught and carried back up to his cave, or to a still more dangerous ledge, and they often bring scraps to starving hermits, though not to those fasting by choice.

The tallest, Agio Pnevma, the Tower of the Holy Ghost, has the strongest aura, and its summit is thought a gate to Heaven; no mortal who reached it ever came back to say so.

Several vis sources are believed to lie here, but magi rarely come. The last one tried to fly up the Agio Pnevma; his levitation failed, perhaps in punishment for his pride, and the vultures ate him.

neighbours.name: Pyrgos Diavolou
neighbours.summary:
The Tower of the Devil, the one unholy pillar of Meteora, with an Infernal aura of 4 and a colony of foul vultures that harry and attack anyone who climbs it.

Some hermits climb it to stay as long as they can, as a test of faith, and it would serve as the ordeal of a Mystery initiation. For forty days and nights, Christ's time in the desert, the vultures torment the climber and three temptations come: stones the birds bring become fresh loaves, agonising poison if eaten; high up, a vulture urges him to leap, since the eagles save the devout, and he dies if he does; and at the summit an alluring vision of the Devil shows him all he longs for, granting an Infernal Blessing if he accepts.

neighbours.name: The Magnesian Coast
neighbours.summary: The south-east of Thessaly, known since antiquity for stones and minerals that alchemists and magi prize, above all the magnes in two kinds. The male magnes, some of them Terram vis, are dark lodestones that pull at iron (+7 to control iron, +3 divination); set one on a scrap of parchment, add a certain powder, and mystic symbols appear. The female, a little paler, are Imaginem vis and make glass perfectly clear when added to it (+3 purification, +2 invisibility). Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: Mount Pelion
neighbours.summary:
A hooked peninsula at Thessaly's south-eastern tip, six miles across and twenty long, with no human settlement: one overgrown, mountainous maze of oak and beech, choked with undergrowth and deadfall, under a Faerie aura of 3, and hard to find one's way through. Here Peleus wed the nymph Thetis, who bore Akhilles.

It is the home of the centaurs, faeries as wild as stallions and as civil as men in equal parts, who challenge intruders to fierce, often deadly contests of fighting, hunting or racing, and celebrate with drunken feasts.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Chiron
neighbours.summary: On Mount Pelion proper, the forest's highest point at the north of the peninsula, the cave of Chiron, first and wisest of the centaurs, unmatched in astrology and medicine and famed for his divinations; he taught Herakles, Asklepios, Akhilles, Theseus, Jason and many more. Seekers and Merinita magi have gone into Pelion to learn from him, and not all of them came back.

neighbours.name: Attica and Boeotia
neighbours.summary: The heartland of ancient Greece: Boeotia, round Thebes, and south of it the peninsula of Attica, round Athens, bitter rivals of old, divided by the wooded limestone hills of Kithaeron, a much-fought border now scattered with faerie sites and the ruins of old forts. Both are the Duchy of Athens, under Otto de la Roche.

neighbours.name: The Kithaeron Mountains
neighbours.summary:
The hills between Boeotia and Attica, backdrop of many battles and legends, now dotted with faerie sites and ruined fortifications (no aura is given).

When Kadmus founded Thebes he slew the dragon there and sowed its teeth as Athene told him; the Spartoi, the 'sown men', sprang up full-grown and armed, children of Ares. Most fought him, five helped him build his city, and when Athens finally beat Thebes their race withdrew to a forgotten spot in these hills, where they may yet remain.

neighbours.name: Mount Parnassos
neighbours.summary: The sacred mountain west of the Boeotian plain, wooded and uninhabited, above Delphi's terraced sanctuary and the Castalian Spring.

neighbours.name: Delphi
neighbours.summary:
The most famous oracle of the ancient world, once asked by kings, emperors, tyrants and philosophers about politics, war and religion, and famed for answers that came true, if often darkly put. It lies on a terraced plateau among crags below Parnassos: the Temple of Apollon at the centre of a small cluster of temples, ruins and an amphitheatre. The oracle itself has a Magic aura of 9, the rest of the sanctuary 7; the omphalos and its ties to the titans make Magic, not Faerie, the stronger here.

It is in the keeping of the Tribunal and the Order. A lone Criamon maga lives here as the oracle under the old ceremonial name, Pythia, and in time picks her successor (often her filia), who after initiation into the oracle's Mysteries takes the name and role without announcement; so, though many magae have served, Pythia is thought of as one lasting being. Magi come to consult her before great ventures, the founding of a covenant or the taking of a patron, and often before important Tribunal decisions. How much of the future she sees, if any, is unclear, but her riddles nearly always prove wise in the end. Supplicants are received only from spring to autumn; they bring money or valuables, and larger gifts later if the prophecy bears fruit.

The temple, which Pythia uses as her laboratory, is richly adorned with these gifts. In its secret inner room, the adyton, is the omphalos, the hollow egg-shaped navel stone carved with a woven net, said to mark the centre of the earth: the stone Rhea swaddled and gave Kronos to swallow in place of Zeus. Vapours rising from a small hole in it are Intellego vis, which Pythia breathes to prophesy; and an eternal flame burns in an inner hearth, a strong Creo vis source, any fire lit from it burning for ever without fuel. Pythia gathers both for the Tribunal, a common source of the polity, after taking what she needs.

Herophile, the Delphic Sibyl, dwells in the same precinct but is not, and never was, the Pythia; she prophesies only for those of royal blood, however thin (see the Bestiary for a sibyl).

Herophile, the Delphic Sibyl, also lives in the sacred precinct; she is not and never was the Pythia, though the two share the place. She prophesies only for those of royal blood, however thin. See also the Erythraean, Samian, Hellespontine and Phrygian sibyls.
neighbours.secrets: The Absent Oracle: visitors may find only a young girl who says she is Pythia's apprentice, that her mistress is away, and repeats a last prophecy that seems to foretell both the disappearance and its rescuers. Whether Pythia has been taken or is being eccentric, the riddle must be solved to bring her back.

neighbours.name: The Castalian Spring
neighbours.summary: A pool at the foot of a great pair of cliffs on the lower slopes of Parnassos, its water and rocks dazzlingly bright, under a Faerie aura of 4. Those going up to the oracle wash their hair here and leave gifts of vis for Pythia in niches cut in the cliff. Their hair seems to soak up some of the light, and trimmed it yields Imaginem vis. Its old guardian was the she-serpent Python, Gaia's daughter, whom Apollon killed.

neighbours.name: The Palace of the Lamia
neighbours.summary: A shore of the Gulf of Corinth some miles south of Parnassos, where a lamia (see the Bestiary) rises from the sea whenever a young man pipes on the beach, and promises him an easy, delightful life at her side. If he refuses she tears him apart; if he accepts she drags him under and drowns him.
neighbours.secrets: Sometimes the man is instead carried to her palace beneath the waves and given that life, and she teaches him many secrets she has gathered: a perilous way to study, with great rewards. Many lamiae can initiate Mystery Virtues.

neighbours.name: Eleusis
neighbours.summary:
The sanctuary of the Eleusinian Mysteries, fourteen miles north-west of Athens, where Demeter found her daughter Kore again and made peace with her fate; King Keleus was among the first initiates. The site has a Magic aura of 4, rising to 6 in the great forty-two-columned telesterion.

Each year initiates walk the Sacred Way from Athens through the Forest of Daphni, drink the kykeon at nightfall, and meet Hekate as a three-handed crone with dagger, golden key and rope; she gives the chosen, the epoptai, a password to the inner rite, and tells the mystai to wait a year. The Lesser Mystery each March grants Self-Confident; the Greater, every fifth August, may grant Death Prophecy (the cult itself is described with the realms).

The rite ends with an all-night feast and bull sacrifice in the Rharian Field, where grain first grew: a potent source of Herbam vis.

neighbours.name: The Tumulus of Marathon
neighbours.summary:
On a small plain in eastern Attica in sight of the Aegean, a big grassy cone, Magic aura 3, over the 192 Athenians who fell beating the Persians; an old stone before it bears Simonides's verse.

Every September, on the anniversary, the ghost of the herald Pheidippides runs the 26 miles to Athens and looks up at the Acropolis. If Greeks rule there he cries victory and dies again, leaving his sandals, each with 3 pawns of Creo vis. If barbarians hold it he turns away silent and fades, and the next nightfall the 192 wake and fight their way across Attica, attacking anything in their path, to storm the Acropolis after a few days.

That is Otto de la Roche's problem: the local Greeks will not fight their own dead, he must hold the city with several hundred crusaders and mercenaries, and as an excommunicate he can expect no help from Heaven. The beaten ghosts leave weapons and gear holding Perdo vis, which the Tribunal has so far declined to gather rather than profit from a Greek defeat, even a symbolic one.
neighbours.secrets: The Perdo vis vanishes soon after the battle, and no one knows who or what is collecting it.

neighbours.name: The Column of St Haralambos
neighbours.summary: A lone column on the road from Athens to Piraeus, raised some generations ago by forty women. They bought a cart and calves and a silver vessel, wrote on it the name of every disease the townsfolk could catch, buried the lot, and set the column over it in honour of St Haralambos, guardian against plague. Athens has had no epidemic since. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Euboea
neighbours.summary:
A long, narrow island shaped like a seahorse, nearly a hundred miles from north-west to south-east, the Tribunal's second largest after Candia, joined to the mainland only by the bridge at Chalkis. It is dry, so farming is poor, but rich in marble. Its Aegean coast is rocky and harbourless, notorious for storms and wicked currents; much of the Persian fleet was wrecked there before Salamis.

William the Bad of Sicily landed ten thousand men from 164 ships in 1157 and sacked every coastal town; the island never recovered and is now thinly peopled. Since the Fourth Crusade it is the Lordship of Negroponte (see the Islands), the Veronese Triarchy's baronies, now split in six under Venetian bailiffs. Aegaea lies on the sea floor off its coast.

Byzantine scholars comparing Homer, Ovid and Apollodorus with the Old Testament hold that Herakles was Samson, and his Labors trials the Devil set him; so places of his virtue tend to be Divine, and those of his foes and Labors Infernal.

neighbours.name: The Euripus Strait
neighbours.summary: The narrows at Chalkis, halfway down the Euboic Sea, little more than a hundred feet wide and crossed by a wooden drawbridge. Its fierce tides change direction many times a day, often without warning; Aristotle tried to explain them, failed, and threw himself in. The genius loci of the Euboic Sea lives in the strait and dreads its being filled in, cutting its sea in two, so it keeps the tides violent to deter mortals. The folk of Chalkis used to keep the bridge up and sail no ships through, to soothe it; the island's new Latin lords are far less careful.

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Euboea
neighbours.summary: Zeus and Hera were married here, and the marriage went so badly that the honour turned to a curse: Hera in a rage wrecked the wedding place with an earthquake that tore Euboea from the mainland and broke its mountain chain into three clumps. Earth spirits war among them, there are several sources of Perdo vis, and earthquakes are still frequent. Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: Aetos
neighbours.summary: A peak near Karystos with a village on each side, Kastania to the east and Neohori to the west, each guarded by a koukouvaoun (a stoicheion; see the Bestiary): Kastania's a cow, Neohori's a golden-horned ox. When the villages quarrel their spirits fight. At the last quarrel Kastania's was pushed over a cliff and buried by a rockslide, and ever since the village has suffered tremors as it struggles to get out, its luck has turned and its crops have failed.

neighbours.name: The Baths of Herakles
neighbours.summary: A hot spring near the north coast, on the slopes of Mount Gaetsades (over four thousand feet), where sulphurous water pours over yellowed rock straight into the sea: one of the places Herakles rested, the healing water springing up to refresh him. Divine aura 4; it cures gout and rheumatism, and medicinal herbs grow on the slopes about it.

neighbours.name: The Morea
neighbours.summary:
The Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece, tied to Attica only by the Isthmus of Corinth, and named for its many moreai, the mulberry trees whose leaves feed the silkworms: a fertile land of silk. It is the Principality of Achaea, twelve small Frankish baronies under Geoffrey II de Villehardouin.

Herakles worked several Labors here: the Nemean Lion at Nemea between Lake Stymphalia and Corinth, the Hydra at the little Lake Lerna in the south-east, the Erymanthian Boar on Mount Erymanthos in the north, the Augean stables in Elis to the west, and the Stymphalian Birds. Copying a Labor is a favourite Gauntlet for Theban apprentices of House Flambeau.

neighbours.name: The Isthmus of Corinth
neighbours.summary:
The rocky neck joining the Morea to Attica, four miles wide at its narrowest, with the Examilion, a six-mile Byzantine wall of the sixth century, just north of it. Ships once crossed it too, triremes hauled by slaves along a paved track, the Diolkos, now a disused ruin; goods are carried across between Corinth's two ports instead.

Roman emperors dreamt of a canal, and Nero began one with six thousand slaves and spades; it died with him. Centuries later the aptly named Severus of House Guernicus took up the idea and made real progress with ritual Perdo Terram before he was Marched. His great cut is still there.

neighbours.name: Angistri
neighbours.summary: A little island of the Saronic Gulf some twenty miles south-east of the Isthmus, plagued by a hen the size of a cow that raids the crops with its huge brood and fouls the fields with its giant droppings. A witch cast out of the main village took her revenge by sowing magic grain; a hen ate it and grew monstrous.

neighbours.name: Lake Stymphalia
neighbours.summary: The Morea's largest lake, twenty miles west of Corinth, ringed and hidden by thick dark forest, with an Infernal aura of 4 and the dreadful stink of black, poisoned water. Herakles drove off the Stymphalian Birds here with Hephaistos's bronze clappers and his arrows, but long after they came back (see the Bestiary), and they have plagued the fields and villages round about ever since: black birds big enough to carry off a small man and fierce enough to kill and eat a grown one, with brass feathers whose spiked tips they shoot, and a metallic shriek. Their coming is a dire omen.

neighbours.name: Arcadia
neighbours.summary: The mountainous heart of the Morea, a thinly peopled forest wilderness, and also a Faerie realm, the realm of new stories and adventures; whichever was named for the other, the higher one climbs in the one, the nearer one comes to the other. Thresholds and guardians of every kind are scattered through it, on peaks, in groves and caves or met on any path, making it one of the easiest ways into the realm, and Merinita magi from all over the Tribunal and beyond love it. A lost traveller or magus stumbling out of the Arcadian wilds with no idea where he is is not a rare sight.

neighbours.name: Vizie
neighbours.summary: A village in the southern foothills of Arcadia, not far from Sparta, of dog-headed cynocephali who farm and keep sheep. Their neighbours steal their grain and goats, so they must go to war to survive, and the peasants round about call them man-eating monsters; peace between the two seems unlikely. If they were baptised and prayed to St Christopher, himself born dog-headed, they would lose their canine looks.

neighbours.name: Celaenea's Laboratory on Mount Cyllene
neighbours.summary: Mount Cyllene in the north of Arcadia, where Hermes is said to have been born. Celaenea of Bonisagus, a Seeker of Hedyosmos obsessed with the god's legends, keeps a secret laboratory here, sure that by divining the nature of Hermes she can reach the very roots of magic. The book gives no aura.
neighbours.secrets: Proximios means to tell her that Lucian of Aegaea hopes to raise the forgotten gods, trusting her love of Hermes to turn her against him and his league.

neighbours.name: Zakynthos
neighbours.summary:
An island twenty miles long in the Ionian Sea west of the Morea, nominally Venice's, and one of the strangest and most superstitious in Greece: faeries and the faerie-blooded abound, and so do Gifted children, so that magi of the Ionian phyle come regularly to look for them. Hardly a native lacks some faerie blood or a small supernatural knack.

Nereids are commoner here than anywhere; whole villages have married them, some of those villages have vanished for years at a time, and nereid blood here makes children fair and families famous for beauty. The drakoi of Zakynthos have one fiery eye and often uncanny sight; their mortal children are ugly, dim, huge or strong, and a drakos father hunting a husband for his graceless daughter is an old joke. Few houses are built, since a passer-by may leave his shadow in the new foundations, and it becomes a pergalio: a black-skinned, blue-eyed faerie child that wanders harmlessly and goes away in time if its help is accepted, but turns jealous and spiteful if refused.

The one-eyed, fire-eyed drakoi here, great stone-throwers, are probably the kyklopes' children, who came up out of Tartaros to live by the volcanoes.

neighbours.name: The Mountain of the Queen of the Nereids
neighbours.summary: The highest peak at the heart of Zakynthos, Faerie aura 6, home of the nereids and their queen, the Great Lady or Mistress of Earth and Sea: largest, wisest and strongest of them, beautiful in a white gown and golden belt, often seen dancing among her nereids in the brooks and pools or before her plain palace. A man struck with her belt goes mute, weak or simple. She takes children away to live with her for many years, though she treats them well. She is mysterious but high-minded, and one may bargain with her for fair dealing or justice.

neighbours.name: The Sanctuary of Epidauros
neighbours.summary:
The old asklepieion on a quiet hillside near the shore of the north-east Morea, in Achaea: a small huddle of ancient Greek buildings in every state of repair, under a Magic aura of 5, where the magi have their sancta. Its heart is the Hall of Repose (the Enkoimeteria), a great shared hall like a hospital where the gravest or most important patients are laid, and which is in Hermetic terms a laboratory specialised in healing and longevity, though it does not look like one.

The other buildings stand empty and crumbling, one of the outermost holding a leper colony. In the hillside is a great theatre unused since Roman times, its acoustics so perfect that the faintest sound on stage carries to the back row; Imaginem vis can be gathered there. Below lies a small town, where the covenfolk live among the townsfolk; its church gives it a Divine aura too weak to trouble the sanctuary.

neighbours.name: The Valley of Erebos
neighbours.summary:
A long, mostly empty valley on the north side of the Cambunian Mountains at the edge of Thessaly, home of the covenant of Erebos. There is no common building: the magi's sancta are strung along several miles of it with no plan, most in hillside and cliff caves, a few in cottages or tree houses. The valley's Magic aura is mostly 2, with other auras in a few spots.

Nearby is a bat-haunted cave complex, once a sanctuary of a chthonic cult of Hecate. The magi harvest Perdo vis from its bats, but have not gone in because of the cultists' traps.
neighbours.secrets: Cyra, the patron, curses anyone entering the valley with ill intent towards Erebos.

neighbours.name: The Hunting Lodge of Gigas
neighbours.summary: A hunting lodge in a small patch of forest at the very northern end of a rich, fertile valley south-west of Sofia, in Bulgarian lands: the most northerly Theban covenant. To draw no notice in this crowded country the lodge is kept small and the magi's sancta are mostly underground. The wood has a weak Magic aura (the book gives no number; 1 here).

neighbours.name: The Nekyomanteion of Mount Minthe
neighbours.summary: The ruins of a nekyomanteion, a shrine of the dead, on the slopes of Mount Minthe in Elis; in antiquity a temple of Hades, one of his few cult centres, for only the Eleans were known to worship him. Below it lies the covenant of Hedyosmos, wholly underground: winding caves joined by twisting passages, each cavern with several entrances, easy to get lost in. Each magus has a cave or several as a sanctum, always shut by a door, and a sanctum mark glows silver for a moment at the touch of anyone with Magic Resistance, so no one trespasses by mistake. The book gives no strength for the Magic aura, which is aligned with Terram and deepens below: this pack assumes 5 in the covenant.

levels.name: The labyrinth
levels.notes: Beneath the covenant's levels, a maze of passages and caverns whose Magic aura is aligned with Terram and grows stronger the further in one goes (the book gives no numbers: this pack assumes 6 at its mouth, more deeper in, with the covenant at 5, as the Aura Boon's example of Hedyosmos suggests, DE p. 184). Somewhere in it a way into the Magic Realm is thought to open, onto the Underworld prison of the titans; Minthe guards a gate into Tartaros. The covenant warns people off, but uses some chambers for its cult.

neighbours.name: The Convent of Koukoubiou
neighbours.summary:
A tiny convent inside Thessaloniki's walls, in a walled villa with a small orchard and a lovely flower garden, kept by Sisters Anna and Theocharista Psellus with six nuns loyal to them. Their private chapel, Divine aura 4, is their laboratory, their prayers and chant the focus of their magic; elsewhere in the villa the aura is 2, and in the walled gardens 1.

The Seirene twins live in the royal palace with only four slaves, using a room of their apartment as a cramped laboratory, and are looking for something better, not least because they quarrel.

neighbours.name: Principality of Epiros
neighbours.summary:
The largest of the new realms of Greece, born of the Greek revolt against the Latins. Its founder, Michael Komnenos Doukas, cousin of the emperors Isaac II and Alexios III, served the Latins in the Morea until William de Champlitte crushed him at the Olive Grove (Koundouros) in 1205; he fell back to Arta and built a realm there, savage and faithless, changing Church and allies at will. He struck at Thessaloniki with Venice in 1210, betraying his son-in-law the infant king, was excommunicated for crucifying three Latin priests, had to bow to Emperor Henry, then from 1213 seized the Adriatic and Ionian coast from Venice, Corfu and Durazzo among it. In 1215 a servant driven past bearing by his cruelty stabbed him, and nobody mourned.

His half-brother Theodore, who fled to Nicaea in 1204 and came over to Epiros in 1210, succeeded him, the bastard son having fled. Theodore is as ruthless and grasping: he has taken Ohrid and Pelagonia from the Bulgarians and most of Thessaly, captured the Latin emperor Peter of Courtenay on the Via Egnatia in 1217 (presumed dead, many of his men murdered or dead in prison), and with a strong army of Frankish mercenaries is closing on Thessaloniki. He has not yet called himself emperor, but Constantinople's throne is plainly his goal, and he holds the western Via Egnatia, by which he could strangle the Latin Empire. The book calls him both Theodore Dukas and Theodore Komnenos.
neighbours.secrets: Arta's new castle has an Infernal aura from Michael's depravities, guarded by a flock of sinister ravens.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary:
Founded by Boniface of Montferrat, who, passed over for the Latin throne, marched on Thessaloniki in 1204 and was hailed as a liberator from bad emperors across Macedonia and Thessaly; his brother Renier's marriage to Maria Komnenos gave him a lawful claim, and his own to Margaret of Hungary, Isaac II's widow, made it firmer. When he died in 1207 his heir was their two-year-old son Demetrios, named for the city's saint, beloved of the great Greek families for his Angelos mother; he was crowned at four in 1209 and is now fifteen.

Margaret's regency was popular until she married Nicholas St Omer of Thebes; Emperor Henry then named his brother Eustace regent, wedded to Michael of Epiros's daughter, forced the Frankish lords who favoured William VI of Montferrat to submit, and saved the boy from a Venetian, Bulgarian and Epirote alliance. After Henry died in 1216 Emperor Peter accepted William's claim and Margaret fled into exile, leaving her son behind; Peter's presumed death at Epirote hands let Demetrios keep his crown. Now Epiros attacks in earnest from the north and west, much land is lost, the fighting is constant, and the city seems unlikely to hold much longer.

Relations with its Greek subjects are far better than the Latin Empire's: Boniface's system still stands, every vassal owing a season of garrison and a season of war each year, Greeks with exactly the same rights and dues as Latins. Its army is mostly Byzantine, with Frankish lords and mercenaries of doubtful loyalty minding their own estates, so a Frankish kingdom with a Greek army fights a Greek principality with a Frankish one. Count Oberto of Biandrate is the boy's deadly enemy.

neighbours.name: Duchy of Athens
neighbours.summary:
Otto de la Roche of Burgundy set up the duchy in 1205 and has styled himself duke since 1208; to the Greeks he is Megas Kyr, Great Lord. He did homage first to Boniface as King of Thessaloniki, supports Demetrios, and has also done homage to the Latin emperor; Athens is deep in the war against both Epiros and the Bulgarians.

A devout Catholic, he founded the Cistercian house at Daphni and has made the Parthenon the Cathedral of Our Lady inside the newly fortified Acropolis, where he lives. He calls Orthodox priests heretics, has turned many out of their posts into poverty and abuses them whenever he can, denying their ordination as a dodge to escape his labour dues and taxes; the pope has excommunicated him for it and demanded amends, and whether he will obey is uncertain. He holds the Image of Edessa, to the fury of Eastern churchmen. As an excommunicate he gets no Divine help against the ghosts of Marathon.

Relic: the Image of Edessa, a napkin-sized piece of Christ's linen shroud bearing the print of His face (Faith 5, Divine Might 50; Celestial Immunity and the Leap of the Faithful), taken from Hagia Sophia and now Otto de la Roche's. Eastern churchmen resent it bitterly; a few appealed to Innocent III, for nothing.

neighbours.name: Lords of Thebes
neighbours.summary: Thebes is held jointly by Otto de la Roche's brother Guy and Nicholas St Omer. In 1207, after Boniface's death, Nicholas married his widow Margaret of Hungary, her third marriage (she had first been Emperor Isaac II Angelos's wife), and the queen lives with him at Thebes.
neighbours.ruler: Guy de la Roche and Nicholas St Omer, jointly

neighbours.name: Principality of Achaea
neighbours.summary:
The Morea's twelve small baronies. Geoffrey I de Villehardouin, shipwrecked at Modon on his way to Syria, fought for a Greek warlord there, fled north when the next one turned on him, and met his old friend William de Champlitte in Boniface's camp; seeing the Morea in near-anarchy, they set out to win it. William's victory at the Olive Grove over an Epirote army ten times larger made the principality in 1204. William died in 1209 on his way home, leaving Geoffrey regent until the heir Robert came within a year and a day; Geoffrey and the Venetians saw that he did not, and Geoffrey took the throne. The Greek resistance faltered after Leo Sgouros rode his horse off the walls of Acrocorinth in 1208, and the whole Morea was taken by 1211; in thanks Geoffrey gave the Cistercians land at Zaraka.

Geoffrey II succeeded in 1218. He is married to Agnes de Courtenay, daughter of the late Empress Yolanda and Emperor Peter, and is on good terms with the Latin Empire and the Venetians, whose trade is making the principality rich. Generous to Greek and Latin alike, he is popular, and unlike Athens's duke he gets on with the Orthodox clergy, excusing them tax and military service while taxing Latin church lands, to the pope's annoyance. Epidauros lies in his lands. The book names no seat; Andravida is history's.
neighbours.secrets: If he falls gravely ill, Agnes will come to Epidauros begging for a cure (Healing the Realm).

neighbours.name: Tsardom of Bulgaria
neighbours.summary:
The northern neighbour of Greece, whose Christian armies once overran it and whose tsar Kaloyan besieged Thessaloniki in 1207, until (the city says) St Demetrios rode out and speared him; the Bulgarians whisper that his Cuman captain murdered him. It has lost Ohrid and Pelagonia to Epiros, and allied with Venice and Epiros against Thessaloniki in 1210. Gigas lies in its lands, in a fertile valley south-west of Sofia.

The book names Boril as the current tsar; history has Ivan Asen II, who deposed him in 1218, ruling in 1220. The book names no capital; Tarnovo is history's.

neighbours.name: Latin Archbishopric of Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary: Its cathedral is the city's Hagia Sophia, a smaller copy of Constantinople's, lately given to the Western Church. The Latin archbishop, who tutored King Demetrios as a boy, is his noted friend and supporter. Orthodox and Latin churches live peaceably side by side in the city, though the Latin hierarchy is on top.

neighbours.name: Hagios Demetrios, Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary:
The city's foremost church, an ancient basilica over the old Roman forum and shrine of its patron, St Demetrios, a martyred Roman soldier whose relics give off the scent of myrrh. His miracles have saved the city from Slav armies many times; if it is gravely threatened he rises from his shrine and fights beside its defenders, and with St George he is patron of the crusades, which may be why the Fourth Crusade wisely left the city alone. The great Fair of St Demetrios is held outside the walls for six days each October, where traders from across Europe meet Arab and Jewish merchants of Africa and the Levant.

Priests still struggle to explain 1185: some say William the Good's war on the vile Andronikos was just and the saint would not rise for such an emperor, even helping the attackers, when the catapults and archers inexplicably ran dry and the walls gave way as if by magic. But he still rises for a just cause: in early October 1207 a shining armoured rider came out against the besieging Bulgarians and killed Tsar Kaloyan with a spear, and many on the walls saw it. He is the patron of Oikos tou Eleous, whose sisters invoked him that day.

neighbours.name: Rotunda of St George, Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary: The oldest church in Greece: squat, round and enormously thick-walled, which has let it outlast the centuries.

neighbours.name: The Holy Community of Mount Athos
neighbours.summary:
The monastic republic of the Holy Mountain, which the Latin rulers have left exactly as it was. Most monasteries join in electing the protos, 'the first', who speaks for the community to the outside world; three, the Great Lavra (founded 955, the first great house), Vatopedi and Iviron, stay independent, and their abbots wield much influence of their own, even beyond the protos's.

Its houses span many peoples: Iviron is Georgian, Panteleemon Russian, Zographou Bulgarian, the Serbs have Hilander, Armenian monks are common, and three Benedictine monasteries of the Latin rite have been built over the centuries. A monstrous drakos once crawled from the sea to settle in the Karakalou monastery.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Ohrid
neighbours.summary: The see of the former Bulgarian capital, with dozens of ancient churches; the Bulgarian Church's head there is now under Epirote rule since Theodore took the city. The placid monastery of St Naum stands on the lake shore.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Larissa
neighbours.summary: Larissa has been an archbishop's seat since the fifth century; it is now in Epirote hands with the rest of Thessaly.

neighbours.name: The Skete of Doupiani, Meteora
neighbours.summary: A small community of hermit monks among the pillars of Meteora, named for the pillar that holds its common chapel of the Theotokos, founded by the first monk, Varnavas, in the tenth century. Some hermits live high in caves and cracks in the sheer rock, where they have painted crude frescoes, and rough rope pulleys haul up food, goods and even men; the ropes are changed only when they break, as God wills.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Daphni
neighbours.summary: Between Athens and Eleusis, on the Sacred Way. Its old Greek monks, friendly to the Eleusinian cult, had made a Christian house of a sanctuary of Apollon (mystics to some, heretics to most), and the procession of initiates stopped there; it was sacked in 1205 and given to the Cistercians, which has made the cult's way harder.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Zaraka
neighbours.summary: Land in Arcadia that Geoffrey I gave the Cistercians in thanks for the conquest of the Morea, where an imposing Gothic monastery is now going up.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Our Lady, Athens
neighbours.summary: The Parthenon, Athene's great temple on the Acropolis, lately made a Latin cathedral by Otto de la Roche, inside the newly walled citadel where he lives; with the Acropolis it is the seat of the duchy.

neighbours.name: Arta
neighbours.summary: Once a minor town, on the site of Corinthian Ambracia (named for an Amazon princess, Apollon's granddaughter) and later King Pyrrhus's capital; Michael Komnenos made it the capital of Epiros after Koundouros, and in fifteen years it has swollen with refugees from the troubled east and south, Constantinople included. Its formidable new castle has an Infernal aura and a guard of sinister ravens, and its churches' Divine auras are weak in proportion. Its market, across the cursed bridge, is a grubby, treacherous place.

neighbours.name: Durazzo
neighbours.summary: Dyrrhachium, the biggest and one of the oldest cities of Epiros, in a sheltered Adriatic harbour, a port since time out of mind with ships running constantly to Italy and Venice, and the west end of the Via Egnatia, so a link between the West and the Orthodox East: busy and cosmopolitan, with Italians, Venetians, Greeks, Bulgars, Jews and Vlachs. Venice took it in 1204; Epiros has since taken it back.

neighbours.name: Corfu
neighbours.summary: Korkyra to the Greeks: the port town halfway down the east shore of the large hilly island off the Epirote coast, Venetian until Michael Komnenos took it in 1214. The Stone Ship stands just outside its harbour.

neighbours.name: Ohrid
neighbours.summary: The venerable episcopal city on Lake Ohrid's north shore, on the Via Egnatia, former capital of the Bulgarian Empire, with dozens of old churches; taken from the Bulgarians by Theodore of Epiros.

neighbours.name: Monastiri
neighbours.summary: An ancient city a dozen miles east of the lakes, under Mount Pelister.

neighbours.name: Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary:
The Co-Queen of the empire, second only to Constantinople: over 100,000 souls, bigger than Paris, founded by King Cassander near old Therma and named for his wife, Alexander's half-sister. St Paul preached in its synagogues and wrote it two epistles, and Cyril and Methodius took the Gospel from here to Bulgaria. A mile-long harbour faces the sea, huge Byzantine walls the other three sides; within are Roman arches and statues, a vast hippodrome, an imperial mint, the Rotunda of St George, the Hagia Sophia (now the Latin cathedral) and above all the Hagios Demetrios. Mostly Greek, with small Italian and Jewish communities.

The Sicilians sacked it in 1185, killing thousands, but it recovered; the Fourth Crusade passed it by, so it keeps much of its Byzantine splendour, a hint of what the Queen of Cities was. Oikos tou Eleous is here; Paulicians live lawfully within the walls; the Gorgona haunts the harbour; and the armies of Epiros close in from north and west.

Saint: Demetrios, the city's patron and the soldiers' (an area saint, Divine Might 50). In 1207, besieged by Ioannitsa the Greek-slayer, tsar of Bulgaria, the city called on him, and he took bodily form and killed the tsar with a spear.

neighbours.name: Serres
neighbours.summary: A castle town of the kingdom where Emperor Henry imprisoned Count Oberto of Biandrate in chains in 1209.

neighbours.name: Larissa
neighbours.summary: The ancient chief city of Thessaly, an archbishop's seat since the fifth century, in the middle of the wide, fertile plain, now ruled from Epiros. It is named for the kindly nymph of a local spring, still sometimes seen and honoured as a saint; she and the horse, for the plain's famous horses and horsemen, are its emblems.

neighbours.name: Thebes
neighbours.summary: The city that names the Tribunal, founded by Kadmus at the south edge of the Boeotian plain on the Delphic oracle's word; its citadel, the Kadmea, bears his name. Alexander razed it, and for a thousand years it was a shadow of itself until silk came in the tenth century: within two centuries its weavers were the empire's best, surpassing Constantinople, with dyes from Athens. Roger II of Sicily carried the whole industry, workers and all, off to Sicily in the twelfth century, so the secret reached the West, but Thebes recovered fully. With 30,000 people, many of them silk growers and weavers, it is easily the second city of Greece. Queen Margaret lives here.
neighbours.ruler: Guy de la Roche and Nicholas St Omer

neighbours.name: Athens
neighbours.summary: So old that its founding is lost: Athene and Poseidon vied to be its patron, and it chose her olive tree over his spring, so olive groves still bless it. Fallen from favour under the Christian empire, it is still a large, prosperous port of about 10,000, often visited by Venetians, with surplus grain and olives, fine dyes and soaps for the silk trade, and the marble quarries of Penteli in the hills nearby. The Acropolis and its new Latin cathedral are the duke's seat. The Column of St Haralambos on the Piraeus road keeps plague away.

neighbours.name: Chalkis
neighbours.summary: Euboea's main town, named for the copper and bronze workers who first lived there; its colonists named the Chalkidiki. A sturdy old fortress commands it, a classic base for invading the mainland, and its wooden drawbridge over the Euripus is the island's only link to Boeotia. Seat of the central barony of Negroponte; the northern sits at Oreoi and the southern at Karystos.

neighbours.name: Corinth
neighbours.summary: Founded by Korinthos, of the sun god's line, beside the Isthmus with ports on both the Saronic and Corinthian gulfs; its temple of Aphrodite once kept thousands of prostitutes, and St Paul wrote its Christians two epistles. Earthquakes, Goths and the Sicilians have ruined it again and again, yet it remains a busy port of 10,000, the largest town of the Morea. The great fortress of Acrocorinth, 1,500 feet up behind it, still commands the Isthmus; Leo Sgouros leapt to his death from its walls in 1208.

neighbours.name: Epidauros
neighbours.summary: The small town below the sanctuary, where the covenfolk of Epidauros live among ordinary folk; its church gives it a Divine aura too weak to trouble the sanctuary above.

neighbours.name: Sofia
neighbours.summary: The Bulgarian city north-east of Gigas's valley, in a busy, well-peopled country where the Tremere keep their lodge small.

neighbours.name: The Montferrat Party
neighbours.summary: The Frankish lords of the Kingdom of Thessaloniki who back the claim of William VI, Marquis of Montferrat, Boniface's son by his first wife Helena del Bosco, against his half-brother the boy king. Their moving spirit, Count Oberto II of Biandrate, forced Queen Margaret from the regency, and in 1209 conspired with Emperor Henry, but when Henry heard Margaret out he saw the justice of her cause and had the count chained in the castle at Serres. Freed years later, Oberto swore revenge on the emperor and still works tirelessly for William; he is King Demetrios's mortal enemy.

details.wants: William VI of Montferrat on the throne of Thessaloniki in place of Demetrios
details.offers: Frankish swords and plots at court

neighbours.secrets: Oberto may have poisoned Henry in 1216, though others blame his Bulgarian empress Maria.

neighbours.name: The Greek Families of Thessaloniki
neighbours.summary: The great Greek houses and citizens of the Co-Queen, who love King Demetrios for his Angelos mother, supported Margaret's regency, and give the kingdom its largely Greek army. Under Boniface's settlement they hold exactly the rights and dues of the Latins, which keeps them loyal to a Frankish crown against the Greek prince of Epiros.

details.wants: Their city kept whole and Byzantine, under a king of Angelos blood
details.offers: The loyalty of the townsfolk, Byzantine troops, money

neighbours.name: The Islands
neighbours.summary:
The Aegean, the sea of the Greek heroes' voyages, and its hundreds of islands, from bare rocks to lands of hundreds of square miles: the Archipelago, as it was called of old and still is. It is named for Aegeus, the Athenian king who drowned himself when his son Theseus forgot the white sail of victory, and also for Aegaea, Poseidon's palace under its waters; the Bulgarians, comparing it with the stormy Black Sea, call it the White Sea. Many islands are green, with vines, orchards, olives and grain, goats and sheep on the heights; the small ones are mostly barren. Some are volcanic, others rich in marble, stone or ore. Windmills, learned from the Muslims during the crusades, grind the corn in the steady winds. Every town that matters is a port, and none is a great city.

After 1204 the islands were shared, on parchment, between Venice and the Latin Empire, but real control varies and has shifted for fifteen years; local despots and even pirates rule some. Venice took the key harbours: Candia, Rodos, Karpathos and the Cyclades, and in the north only Lemnos, Ingasia's island, which makes some magi suspect House Verditius of a secret bargain with the old doge, or of helping the crusade.

Piracy is ancient here and has hardly changed: booty, and captives held for ransom. Dionysos himself was once seized by Tyrrhenian pirates, and turned their oars to snakes and the men to dolphins. On the poorer islets raiding is a way of life with no shame in it, though every lord hangs pirates when he can. The empire's collapse has swelled their numbers, and some pirate chiefs now rule ports, checked only by the crusaders and the Venetian fleet; some Venetian captains will deal with pirates who prey on their rivals. The Tribunal forbids covenants to attack one another's ships, but not to rob mundanes, though that is frowned on.

The islands have always been places of exile: early Christians under Rome, then pagans, heretics, criminals and traitors under the Byzantines, and wicked hedge wizards with the beasts and demons they called up, many of them bound by the old Byzantine magicians. Since Constantinople fell those old bindings have been failing, and many of the menaces are loose again. Covens of stringles infest several small isles (see the realms), and islanders bury the cursed on bare islets so they cannot rise as vrykolakes.

Vis of the islands, each described in its place: the stone roots of Lesbos's Petrified Forest (Perdo), Ikaria's healing springs (Creo), the bows of Delos's nymphs (Rego, see the Bestiary), the springs of Naxos, the mane of Keos's stone lion (Rego), Thera's pumice (Perdo), the echo in St John's cave on Patmos (Intellego), the old wreath of the Tree of Hippocrates on Kos (8 Creo), the Colossus's bronze shards on Rodos (Ignem), the acorns of Mount Zeus's oak (Vim) and Talos's ichor on Candia (7 Ignem). The book does not say which of them are the polity's common sources.

Of the Tribunal's phylai, the Aegean takes in the northern islands with Aegaea and Ingasia; the Kretan takes in Candia, the Cyclades and the Dodecanese, with Favonius and Polyaigos.

neighbours.name: The burial islets
neighbours.summary: Small empty islets off the settled islands where wise islanders bury those cursed or wicked in life, so they will not come back as vrykolakes (see the Bestiary). Many hold tumbledown graveyards with an Infernal aura (the book gives no strength) and are plagued by the vampires, whom the sea usually keeps from the inhabited shores.

neighbours.name: The North Aegean
neighbours.summary: The northern half of the Archipelago. Its western waters have few large islands save the Sporades, wooded and farmed; to the east a chain of bigger islands follows the Asian shore, all nominally the Latin Empire's except Venetian Lemnos. Among the beings met here are the Gorgona (see Greece) and the magi of Aegaea with their tritones. In size after Lesbos come Khios, Lemnos, Samos, Thasos, Imbros, Ikaria and Samothraki.

neighbours.name: Lesbos
neighbours.summary:
The third island of Greece in size, after Candia and Euboea: green and pleasant, full of gardens and flowers, with two great inlets, two mountains and several hot springs. It is famed for minstrels, poets and lovers, and here, unusually, women stand above men. Five of its old towns, Mytilene, Mithymna, Issa, Antissa and Avrisi, bear the names of the daughters of King Makaras, son of Helios, who each ruled one, and the island's women have ruled ever since; it took its name from Lesbos, one of his sons-in-law. Cybele was worshipped here of old, and her male devotees unmanned themselves and lived as women.

Sappho, the poetess of the sixth century BC, was born here; the ancients called her the tenth Muse, but she wrote in obscure Aeolic and Byzantine scholars now neglect her. Her spirit still walks the gardens, inspiring poets and lovers, and would suit a covenant here as patron. Aristotle wrote his History of Animals and four related works on the island; Rome and Byzantium neglected it and used it for exiles, Empress Irene of Athens among them in 802.

A native who keeps Lesbos's ways abroad, the domineering woman or the meek man, should take Social Handicap; Enchanting Music and Free Expression are common.

neighbours.name: Orphykia
neighbours.summary:
The sacred grove of Orpheus on the westernmost shore of Lesbos, near Antissa. When the maenads tore the singer apart, his head and lyre were carried by a river to the sea and washed up here; the islanders buried the head with honour in the middle of a rich shrine, and Terpander of Antissa, the great minstrel who made the seven-stringed lyre, took the lyre for himself. Now it is an idyllic garden with a Magic aura of 4, where the nightingales sing better than anywhere known, and Sappho's spirit often lingers.

It is holy to the Cult of Orpheus (Houses of Hermes: Societates), and a lone magus of that tradition, Zacharias of House Ex Miscellanea, keeps it.

neighbours.name: The Petrified Forest of Lesbos
neighbours.summary: A desolate vale in western Lesbos where a forest has turned to stone: trunks of all sizes stand upright, and a few of the stone pillars look much like cursed woodcutters. A spiteful band of kalotyches, the tree spirits who avenge a felling (see the Faerie landscape), lives here, and the place, with its Faerie aura of 3, is dreaded across the island.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: the stone roots of the trees can be cut as Perdo vis, which angers the spirits. For fear of sharing the woodcutters' fate the islanders honour their trees and never fell them, one reason Lesbos has so many tended gardens and groves.

neighbours.name: Khios
neighbours.summary: A dry, mountainous island, with vines in its best corners and the mastic bush, a prized spice that yields a chewing gum and grows nowhere else. Its black medicinal wine, first grown by King Oenopion, a son of Dionysos, is among the Tribunal's best. Nea Moni, the 'new monastery' founded by Constantine IX, is one of the largest religious houses of the old empire.

neighbours.name: Lemnos
neighbours.summary:
A fertile volcanic island of grain, olives and sheep, shaped like an upturned U round a deep bay on its southern side. Most of it is flat fields, gentle pastures and olive groves, with sandy beaches and well-peopled ports; the largest towns are Myrina on the west coast and Hephaistia on the north-east. The north-western corner is rockier, with the two highest peaks, Mount Vigla and the volcano Mosychlos, home of Ingasia and one of the Forges of Hephaistos, a cult site of House Verditius.

Venice has held it since 1204 and has taken the island's products for itself, above all the Lemnian Earth (Lemnia Sphragis), a reddish clay dug near Hephaistia and used to stop bleeding and treat snakebite, which once enriched Ingasia.

neighbours.name: Mount Mosychlos and the Forge of Hephaistos
neighbours.summary:
The active volcano of Lemnos, quiet for centuries, and the seat of Ingasia. Stone houses dot its slopes; a large stone hall is both the covenant's meeting room and the mouth of a labyrinth that runs all through the mountain, with hidden tunnels and secret caverns the present magi have never fully explored. At its heart, close to the molten core, is the Forge of Hephaistos, the centre of a Magic aura of 4, now a shared Hermetic laboratory that gives +8 to Rego and +5 to making enchanted items.

The volcano's genius loci, Mosychlos, is the covenant's patron. His temper can shake the ground and bring down tunnels, or send lava into the passages nearest the core; the magi's devices hold back the magma and prop the tunnels while they stay in place.

neighbours.name: Samos
neighbours.summary: A green island thick with vineyards and olive groves, where Hera was born; the ruins of her great temple, the Heraion, stand here. The Tunnel of Eupalinos, an ancient aqueduct cut wonderfully straight for over a thousand yards under a mountain, was built with the help of Pythagoras, a Samian.

neighbours.name: Thasos
neighbours.summary: Four miles off the Macedonian shore, an island rich in mines of silver, gold and lead, and in marble quarries.

neighbours.name: The stable of Pegasus off Imbros
neighbours.summary: Rumour has it that a great sea cave just off Imbros, near the narrow mouth of the Sea of Marmara, is where Pegasus, Poseidon's winged son, is stabled.

neighbours.name: The healing springs of Ikaria
neighbours.summary: Ikaria is named for Icarus, who fell when the sun melted his wax wings. Its famous springs cure barrenness, and Creo vis may be gathered there.

neighbours.name: Samothraki
neighbours.summary: A mountainous granite island with no natural harbour, home of the half-ruined Sanctuary of the Great Gods, centre in antiquity of a mystery cult as popular as the more secretive Eleusinian one (see Greece). A sunken city lies off the east coast; the sponge-divers knew it well and dived there until a monster guarding it ate one who went too near.
neighbours.secrets: The islanders notice occasional visitors who are always dripping wet, and suspect they come from the drowned city.

neighbours.name: The Cyclades
neighbours.summary:
The Encircling Isles, several dozen islands in the middle of the Aegean south-east of Attica and Euboea, said to have been spun round Delos, birthplace of Apollon and Artemis. Cypresses sacred to Artemis grow everywhere, and since they are trees of Hades and resurrection too they cluster by graveyards. In the middle of every village stands an old plane tree, carefully kept: a kalotyche lives in it and blesses the village with sweet vines, herbs and flowers as long as no one harms it. The northerly Etesian winds that cool the summers were Zeus's gift after sacrifices on Keos.

The islands now make up the Duchy of Naxos. In size after Naxos come Andros, Paros, Melos, Keos, Ios, Thermia and Mykonos; Thera lies at the southern end, and Polyaigos off Melos.

neighbours.name: Delos
neighbours.summary:
A small barren island, a mile or two across, once the seat of the Delian League and now forgotten: no people, nothing to take, no strategic worth. That is why so few mortals have noticed that it has torn free of the sea bed and floats wherever the Aegean and Kretan currents take it. The Theban Tribunal has met here since it began; Thebes and other sites were proposed, each by a faction seeking advantage, and Delos won for its history, its empty shores and its aura. It belongs, in name, to the Duchy of Naxos.

Its legend. The titaness Asteria, sister of Leto and mother of Hekate, fled Zeus's advances as a quail and fell into the sea as a floating island (hence its old names Asteria and Ortygia, from ortyx, quail). When Hera swore that the pregnant Leto would find rest on neither land nor sea, the drifting island was neither, and Leto bore Apollon and Artemis there; in thanks she pinned it to the sea floor with four great columns, and Zeus decreed that no one should be born or die on it again. Only the priests of Artemis, Apollon, Leto and Dionysos lived here, with three nymphs Apollon brought from Hyperborea; predators were banned to protect the sacred quail, still plentiful. The League kept its treasury at Apollon's temple, and markets for goods and slaves flourished, but with no food, timber or much water the island emptied, and it has been deserted for at least a thousand years. Some time between eight and twelve centuries ago it began to float again; Hermetic study suggests Leto's binding weakened, but the titans' magic is little understood.

Its aura. Magic outweighs Faerie, since Asteria was of Magic: the whole island has a Magic aura of 3, rising to 8 in places such as the sacred lake, and there are Faerie auras or regiones at the abandoned shrines of Apollon (the book gives no strengths). The aura is aligned to restlessness: anyone ashore gains Restless +1 (+2 where the aura is above 3), magi included. Quail, hares and lizards never stop moving, plants sprout, fruit and wither regardless of season, and visitors never want to stay; magi at a meeting pace about or slip out of the agora, and leave quickly once it ends.

Its wanderings. Delos follows the currents, south in summer and east-north-east in winter, turning clockwise through the Cyclades within roughly the bounds of Astipalaia, Thera, Melos and Andros, and comes back to its old berth between Mykonos and Syros every 19 years. Redcaps crossing the Cyclades watch for it, so the Tribunal can chart it roughly.

The Hyperborean nymphs. Arge, Opis and Loxo, embodiments of archery (distance, aim and flight), came with Apollon and Artemis and still guard the shrines (see the Bestiary). Disturbing a structure or relic calls them out, and vandals have moments to explain before the arrows fly; the wounded do not die until they have left the island. Two more sisters, Hyperoche and Laodice, brought sacred offerings from Hyperborea and vanished on the way home; the three long for news of them. They speak Hyperborean, and seekers of Hyperborean magic (Ancient Magic) may find answers in Apollon's temple or from them, if they prove worthy.

The Tribunal's customs here. Zeus's ban on birth and death is thought to hold still: it is generations since anyone tried to kill here, and every magus present stopped it, fearing Olympian wrath. So no pregnant woman or beast may come to a meeting, and every predator is barred, familiars and companions included; Bjornaer with predatory heartbeasts avoid taking that shape here.

The agora. The meetings are held in the Delian League's old assembly place, a natural bowl lined with marble steps and ringed with carved marble pillars.

The four phyle houses. At a distance from the agora stand the walls of four large buildings and several huts; before each meeting they are roofed and mended, and each phyle shares one of the four with its staff. Tables, chairs and bedding must all be brought from elsewhere. On Mount Kynthos, at the island's centre, among the ruins of the Sanctuary of the Foreign Gods (shrines to Egyptian and eastern deities raised by foreign visitors), a few houses lodge the metoikoi.

The treasury. On the very spot of the Delian League's treasury, a little temple-like building, empty above but for a great leaden trapdoor in the floor, copied from the trapdoor of Bonisagus's tower at Durenmar, never breached and opened only by a big iron key the archon keeps (a ceremonial charge, as the vault is seldom opened between meetings except in emergency). Stairs go down to dusty chambers far underground, where several hundred pawns of vis and many old items and texts are stored and catalogued; so much vis together makes spontaneous magical effects common. The nymphs guard it as they guard every sacred site here. The tamias draws the next seven years' vis from it at each meeting.

The sacred lake. Its shore, with a Magic aura of 8, is where the Ceremony of Propitiation is held after the Rite of Dismissal: each covenant has raised a plinth at the water's edge, holding or awaiting an Arcane Connection to its patron (or the patron itself). The archon opens the rite with an old Ritual from a Casting Tablet, paid with eight pawns of Creo or Vim vis from the Tribunal, which wakes the lake's power; each covenant then tells its patron's deeds, renews its dedication and casts an offering, mostly vis, into the water. The League Against Idolatry boycotts it.

Preparing a meeting. The phyle whose turn it is readies the site, and the work falls to its youngest magi: food for sixty magi and their servants for a week, and seven years of decay, since everything perishable rots fast here; repairs anger the nymphs, who hate any change to the island. Magical beasts drawn by the aura on its wanderings are often stranded on it, and must be driven off, not killed, and kept from the agora by wards, which the phyle teaches its young magi or lends them on Casting Tablets.
neighbours.secrets: The vault is less safe than it looks: a clever magus could rob it, or a dishonest arche skim from it, without great difficulty. No one thinks it has ever happened, and it would be judged a grave crime.

neighbours.name: The island of Naxos
neighbours.summary: The largest and most fertile of the Cyclades, in their middle, and the duke's seat: Marco Sanudo has just finished his strong fortress, the Kastro, and is starting a cathedral. On Mount Zas, the highest peak of the islands, a huge cave like a cathedral was sacred to Dionysos, who wed Ariadne there after Theseus left her on the island.

neighbours.name: The springs of Krini and Karava
neighbours.summary: Two rival springs in the north-east of Naxos. The spring of Krini at Apeiranthos has a shape-changing stoicheion (see the Faerie landscape); that of nearby Karava always appears as a white cat. Karava is the stronger faerie, Krini the more versatile.
neighbours.secrets:
When anyone takes an interest in the springs, Krini turns into a white cat, passes itself off as Karava, and grants leave to take vis from Karava's spring.

Vis: the springs yield vis to those their guardians allow (the book names neither Art nor amount).

neighbours.name: The island of Andros
neighbours.summary: The other great port of the Cyclades, famous for its shipwrights, and the home port of the ship-borne covenant of Favonius, whose founder Memnos keeps his shipyard here.

neighbours.name: Memnos's shipyard
neighbours.summary:
The island workshop of Memnos of Verditius, builder of the Favonius fleet, on the Andros shore: where the felled oak forest of the spirit Dryops was brought, where each sanctum ship was laid down, and where a fifth and last magical ship for the covenant is now on the stocks. His laboratory here has many specialisations and improvements, and four forge-companions work with him. He rarely lacks a commission for a sea-going vessel.

The fifth ship is to carry three laboratories, and the book offers it as a home for a troupe's magi.
neighbours.secrets: Memnos never sails: a Death Prophecy says he will die with the sky above him and the sea below.

neighbours.name: The quarries of Paros
neighbours.summary: The source of translucent white Parian marble, cut in antiquity by tens of thousands of slaves; the quarries are now mostly idle.

neighbours.name: Melos
neighbours.summary: With Thera, one of the two volcanic Cyclades: fertile, rich in obsidian, and full of hot springs, odd caves and striking pillars of rock. Polyaigos, three miles off, buys most of its everyday goods here, and several of its covenfolk keep wives and families on the island.

neighbours.name: Keos and Leon Petrino
neighbours.summary: An island of sweet black wine and many springs, whose nymphs were driven out long ago by a huge lion, Leon Petrino, which seems carved from the mountainside and comes to life to defend Keos. Vis: whoever beats it may cut stones from its mane as Rego vis.

neighbours.name: Ios
neighbours.summary: Where Homer is buried: an island under thick oak forest, the best ship timber in the Archipelago.

neighbours.name: Vryokastro on Thermia
neighbours.summary:
Thermia, named for its hot springs, is barren; on it lies Vryokastro, a ruined town of huge stones raised by the drakoi (see the Faerie landscape), now haunted by more vrykolakes than anywhere else in Greece (see the Bestiary). They lived on Hydra in the Saronic Gulf until a bishop banished them here. They pass as men among the islanders; once a year those of the nearby isles gather on Thermia and show their true shapes to one another, before the dupes they lured along. Most of those are eaten; a few are left mad and let go, to keep Thermia in terror.

A blight on a whole island like this might draw the magi of the Donatores Requietis Aeternae (Houses of Hermes: Societates). The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Mykonos
neighbours.summary: An island strewn with great boulders, said to be giants turned to stone by Herakles. Several covens of stringles infest it (see the realms), and it is thought the capital of their 'kingdom'. Stringles elsewhere in Greece are said to summon a Mykonian demon to help them, at the price of an infant tithed to the witches of Mykonos each year.

neighbours.name: The Bay of Thera
neighbours.summary:
Thera, the southernmost of the Cyclades, newly called Santorini (St Irene) by the Latins, is a crescent of rock round a lagoon that would be a vast harbour but for its sheer black cliffs; a few hamlets perch on top. The still blue bay, several miles across and entered by two wide channels, is fathomless save at its centre, where a volcano's peak smoulders just under the surface. It was land until the last battle of titans and Olympians blew it apart, more than a thousand years before Christ, sending a wave to wreck the coasts of the Cyclades and Candia (see the Magical landscape). Zeus cast Typhon of the hundred serpent heads into Tartaros, and he lies imprisoned in the volcano, now and then belching a whirl of dust and fire that sweeps the whole Aegean. The lagoon has a Magic aura of 7.

Outside the bay the Thalassomachos, the Warrior of the Sea (see the Faerie landscape), haunts the waters, stealing fishermen's nets and raising contrary winds; he never enters the bay, and if he suddenly flees Thera, a great storm from Typhon may be coming.
neighbours.secrets:
The Seekers of the Fallen believe that clearing the mouth of the sunken volcano would open a way into Tartaros, part of the Magic Realm.

Vis: the burning pumice the cloud scatters is Perdo vis.

neighbours.name: The Dodecanese
neighbours.summary: Some two dozen islands in the south-east of the Aegean, the edge of the Greek world in antiquity. Christianity rooted here before anywhere else in the Tribunal, through the missions of St Paul and St John; Muslim rulers left their mark on some islands, but Byzantium's is stronger and newer, in forts, monasteries and churches everywhere. Save Rodos, Karpathos and their neighbours, claimed by Venice, the Dodecanese are the Latin Empire's, though the nearest Asian shores are split between Nicaea and the Seljuks.

neighbours.name: Patmos
neighbours.summary:
A little island at the north of the Dodecanese, the holiest in Greece: St John the Apostle was exiled here, fresh from Nero's persecutions, and a baptismal font marks where he came ashore. Save the monastery of St John the Divine, it is empty of people, but crowded with pilgrims. The book gives no aura.

Saint: Leontios, patron of the monastery of St John the Evangelist, a holy fool who was never a monk and was made a saint for his austerities alone (local, Divine Might 25).

neighbours.name: The Cave of the Apocalypse
neighbours.summary: A small cave high on Patmos's tallest peak, where St John received the visions of the Revelation, written down by his disciple Prochorus. Pilgrims see the stone he slept on, the cross he cut in the rock and the triple cleft through which he heard Christ's voice. Some monks of the monastery claim visions of their own here. The book gives no aura.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: a visiting Criamon magus once caught the murmuring echo from the cleft in a velvet bag, and it proved to be Intellego vis.

neighbours.name: The island of Kos
neighbours.summary: In antiquity one of the richest ports, famed for wine, an ally of Egypt and favourite of its kings (Ptolemy II was born here); under Byzantium still a busy harbour with rich farms. In the war of titans and gods, Poseidon broke off part of Kos and threw it at the titan Polybotes, who lies pinned beneath it: the islet of Nisyros, just south. A Divine aura covers the town (the book gives no strength).

neighbours.name: The Tree of Hippocrates
neighbours.summary: An ancient plane tree in the middle of Kos town, the oldest and biggest in the Tribunal. Settlers from Epidauros set up an asklepieion on Kos, and there Hippocrates, a native, learnt healing from Asklepios and taught it in the tree's shade; later St Paul preached under it. Each autumn the women of Kos weave a wreath of its leaves, which is blessed and hung among the church's icons, and carry the last year's wreath in procession to the shore and throw it into the sea; returning, they hug the tree, which grants them long years and strength. The tree has a Magic aura of 4 inside the town's Divine aura.
neighbours.secrets:
A magus usually waits unobtrusively in a boat to fish the wreath out of the sea.

Vis: the old wreath holds 8 pawns of Creo vis.

neighbours.name: Nisyros
neighbours.summary: The islet south of Kos that Poseidon tore from it and hurled at the titan Polybotes, who is trapped under it still. It has a Magic aura of 3.

neighbours.name: The island of Rodos
neighbours.summary:
The largest of the Dodecanese, named for the nymph Rhode, daughter of Aphrodite and consort of Helios; both were its protectors, and her gift, the pink hibiscus called rhoda, blooms on every shore. The Colossus, a giant Helios astride the harbour mouth and one of the Seven Wonders, stood less than a century before an earthquake broke it at the knees; the bronze lay for centuries until the Saracens broke it up in the seventh century and sold it to a mysterious Jewish merchant from the Holy Land, who took it away on a thousand camels.

The Saracens walled the city and split it into quarters, one still largely Jewish, with another for its rulers. The First Crusade gave it back to Byzantium; Richard the Lionheart took it in 1191 and enlisted its sailors; Venice, whose fleet has kept a base here since 1082, claimed it after 1204. Leo Gavalas, a rich and corrupt dynatos of Constantinople, now rules it as self-proclaimed despot. Fearing that free reading breeds rebellion, he seized every book on the island; only works he approves, which flatter him, may be sold.
neighbours.secrets:
The despot's closest adviser is a hedge wizard of foul character, very likely Infernal, who bends him to his own ends; he wrote the only books left on the island, tainted works including a corrupted Bible, and is greedily hoarding the island's vis while his demon master watches, pleased. Rumours of depravity and sorcery on Rodos may lead the Tribunal to ask for volunteers to look into it (The Despot's Advisor).

Vis: small bronze shards of the Colossus can still be found, and are Ignem vis; perhaps the merchant knew it.

neighbours.name: Candia
neighbours.summary:
Creta in Latin: the largest island of Greece and second of the eastern Mediterranean after Cyprus, the Tribunal's southern edge, some two hundred miles north of Africa. Mountains and rock cover most of it; their streams water the greener plains and plateaus with their olive groves, and sheep and goats graze the hills.

Minos, son of Zeus and Europa and after death a judge of the dead, founded its ancient kingdom. His grandson Idomeneus, a leader at Troy, vowed Poseidon the first living thing he met on coming home if the god saved his ship, met his own son, killed him, and brought a curse on himself and the island.

Rome, Byzantium and the Saracens held it in turn until Nikephoros II won it back in the tenth century. After 1204 it fell to Boniface of Montferrat, who sold it to Venice for 1000 marks; the Genoese pirate Enrico Pescatore held it for years until Venice made good its claim in 1212 and set up the Kingdom of Candia. Venetian families have been settled on it since, under four successive dukes of two years each, and the Greeks seethe at the ports' new taxes and tolls.

Talos, the bronze guardian of Candia, walks again (see the Bestiary): bound for centuries in a cellar of Knossos by the Byzantines, he was freed when the old spell failed, circles the island three times a day hurling rocks at hostile ships, and grips any who land in a red-hot embrace. Vis: drained, his ichor is 7 pawns of Ignem vis. He has become a scourge of Venetian shipping, and the island's rulers offer a fine reward for this 'demon'; House Verditius would want to know what he really is, and he might make a covenant's patron.

neighbours.name: Mount Zeus
neighbours.summary: The mountain behind Chandax: from the sea it shows the huge profile of Zeus's face turned to the sky, though Christian Cretans prefer to see God's. Candia is Zeus's island, where he was born and raised, and the old belief is that he is born anew each year in his cave on Ida, grows up, and dies each winter here. Vis: the acorns of the mountain's single oak are a strong source of Vim vis.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Zeus on Mount Ida
neighbours.summary: Somewhere on the slopes of Mount Ida, Candia's highest peak, the mountain of the Mother Goddess, is the cave where Rhea hid the newborn Zeus from Kronos and three nymphs raised him, beating spears on shields to drown his cries. It has a Faerie aura of 8. A golden dog guards it, and the great eagles that gave Zeus his thunder patrol the heights. Lucian the Scholar of Aegaea claims to have met the nymphs and the infant god on his travels here.

neighbours.name: The Labyrinth of Knossos
neighbours.summary:
The ruins of Candia's ancient capital on a hillside near Chandax, setting of many legends. Poseidon gave Minos a splendid white bull for sacrifice; the king kept it, and the god made Queen Pasiphae desire it, so Daidalos built her a wooden cow, and she bore the bull-headed Minotaur. The bull ravaged the island until Herakles caught it in his seventh labour. Daidalos built the palace, a maze of more than a thousand rooms, to hide the Minotaur, and after Zeus helped Minos against Athens the city sent seven youths and seven maidens a year to feed it; prisoners were turned loose there too, freed if they found the way out. The double axe, the labrys that gave the labyrinth its name, was a sign of protection.

The ruins have a Magic aura of 3 over a weaker Faerie one. Marcus Tauros of House Criamon, who has had visions of a past life as a Minoan priest, may be met here searching the catacombs beneath for what a magical bull cult of the Minoans knew.

levels.name: The intact labyrinth
levels.notes: The highest level of a regio in the ruins, where the palace stands whole; bull and labrys emblems are everywhere inside, and the old tales (Glaukos raised by Polyeidos's herb, Theseus and the Minotaur, Daidalos and Icarus) may be played out again.

neighbours.secrets: Marcus has not yet found that the whole labyrinth survives inside a regio, whose highest level has a Faerie aura of 6. Talos was bound in one of the cellars until lately.

neighbours.name: The Gorge of Apollon
neighbours.summary: The greatest gorge in Europe, over ten miles long, cut by a river from the White Mountains of western Candia; going through it, from over 4000 feet at the north end down to the southern shore, is a hard journey of two days or more along its walls and floor. A Magic aura of 2 runs its whole length. Caves and springs, homes of nereids, old cypresses and pines line the way, with healing mountain flowers: the peony, named for Paion, physician of the gods, who healed Hades and Ares with it; dittany, which wild ibex chew to heal their wounds; and the dark dragon arum, a poison to all but snakes, flower of Hades.

neighbours.name: Keno
neighbours.summary: Halfway down the gorge, where the cliffs tower a thousand feet but stand only a dozen apart, great bronze gates close the way. Beyond lies the hamlet of Keno, with a Faerie aura of 4, where an ancient Cretan people worship Apollon at a temple in its middle. They speak Classical Greek in a Doric dialect, are superb archers and hunters, and know almost nothing of the world. Apollon hid here from Zeus's anger after killing Python, Delphi's guardian, and fell in love with a local nymph and forgot to raise the sun on time; to this day the sun reaches the gorge's heart only at noon.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Poseidon
neighbours.summary:
A Faerie regio on the floor of the Aegean, not far off the coast of Euboea, whose upper level (Faerie aura 8) holds what is taken for Poseidon's palace amid lavish gardens of sea flowers in countless colours and plants with sea-green, shimmering leaves. The palace is a sprawl of open courts, halls and towers, Greek in style but laid out more like a sultan's: white coral and shell lined with silver and gold, floors of a creamy, pearly stone set with gems. The magi have their sancta in some of its grandest rooms and towers. Honoured guests are received in the great central hall, an airy throne room of Doric columns, where Poseidon's throne stands empty at the far end.

Tritones, mermen with green hair and eyes, attend the palace; a lovely nereid, half maiden and half fish (see the Faerie landscape), may be found resting here and there, and sea lions, dolphins, strange fish and sea serpents drift through unconcerned. Grand stables breed fine horses, every one with some faerie blood, which the covenant now and then gives to other magi; on land their nature can show in unexpected ways.

levels.name: The palace and its gardens
levels.enter: Through the sea, by the covenant's leave: Redcaps use Alexandria's glass submarine, or Aegaea's own devices, and call the covenant with its conch
levels.notes: The water of this level is airy: mortals breathe, ink dries and fire burns, and one may walk or swim. It is lit by constant sunshine, as if the surface were a few dozen feet above, though it lies hundreds of feet down.

neighbours.name: The Philomela
neighbours.summary: Memnos's first ship, of Dryops's wood, holding two laboratories in her regio.

levels.name: The hidden laboratories
levels.enter: By a secret way built into the ship
levels.notes: A regio exactly the size of the ship, holding the magi's laboratories.

neighbours.name: The Tereus
neighbours.summary: The second sanctum ship, of Dryops's wood, holding three laboratories in her regio.

levels.name: The hidden laboratories
levels.enter: By a secret way built into the ship
levels.notes: A regio exactly the size of the ship, holding the magi's laboratories.

neighbours.name: The fleet of Favonius
neighbours.summary:
Four round ships and a dozen or so lesser vessels, always on the move round the Aegean, with Andros as home port. The two sanctum ships built of Dryops's wood each carry a Magic aura and a regio of exactly the ship's size: the magi live on the mundane level, in a Magic aura of 2, and work in the regio above it, with a Magic aura of 3, reached by a secret way.

The Philomela, Memnos's first, 72 feet long, holds two laboratories; her captain is Verecunda, and her timbers, enchanted to command the wind at the captain's will, set the fleet's pace and course. The Tereus, 18 feet longer, holds three, under Aeliophanes. The Procne, 60 feet long, is the covenant's main trader, an ordinary Aegean round ship with one deck almost all hold, under Basil of Andros. The Halcyon, 115 feet by 40, little better than a barge and the clumsiest of them, is the magi's meeting place and the store for their costliest and most fragile goods; it sails in the middle of the fleet, its spells calming rough seas around it. Some of the other ships are Memnos's early work, with Sails and Rudders of Quality or small charms of speed and handling.

Each main ship is a structure of Excellent Quality (City & Guild): +2 to navigation and ship-handling. The Tereus and the Halcyon are Size +9 with 16 damage levels; the Philomela is Size +8 and the Procne +7, with 12 each. All four are warded against fire and mend themselves by taking in new wood; they are bought with the Magical Fortress Boon, so their enchantments cost no covenant Build Points.

neighbours.name: Polyaigos
neighbours.summary:
