A little rocky, mostly barren island at the Cyclades' western edge, three miles by four, with two peaks of a thousand feet; its name means 'many goats', and wild goats overrun it. On the higher peak the magi have built a watchtower that is also their council chamber and library. Below it eight dragon-houses (drakos-houses) stand at equal distances in an octagon, one due north of the peak, the next north-east, and so on: squat, rough cones of great boulders and slates, very strong, each of two floors, home and laboratory. Laskaris had an expert in Hermetic Architecture place them and raise a Magic aura in place of the Infernal one, and Varazes heaved the boulders from all over the island. The Magic aura round the peak and the sancta has grown to 4.

In a flat green spot in the middle of the island is the covenfolk's stone village: a square bell tower ringed by four pavilions for drill and teaching, then barracks, kitchens, stables, workshops and lodgings. Ruined houses of the giants, some now mere heaps of boulders, are scattered about. The covenant's warship lies in the small harbour. There is no other settlement; Melos, larger and greener, lies three miles west.

neighbours.name: Stroggylo, the house of Varazes
neighbours.summary: The lower peak of Polyaigos, crowned by a bigger dragon-house where the covenant's patron, the drakos Varazes, lives, in a Faerie aura of 2.

neighbours.name: Argentiera
neighbours.summary: An island just over a mile north-west of Polyaigos, named for its prized silvery stone, where the covenant holds a monopoly of the quarrying.

neighbours.name: The mines of Sifnos
neighbours.summary: An island a little north of Argentiera, with ancient gold and silver mines long abandoned.
neighbours.secrets: Polyaigos has quietly reopened them.

neighbours.name: Duchy of Naxos
neighbours.summary:
The new realm of the Cyclades. Marco Sanudo, a Venetian, nephew of Doge Enrico Dandolo of the Fourth Crusade and heir to much of his charm and good sense, was charged with putting down Cycladic piracy; he borrowed Venetian galleys, fell on Naxos in 1207 and, after hard fighting, took it, and by 1212 he held nearly all the Cyclades, which he split into more than fifty lordships under him, many held by his kin. Delos is his, in name.

The duchy thrives: it does homage to the Latin emperor and is mostly left alone in the endless wars and intrigues. In name a vassal of the Latin Empire, Marco holds his lands in his own right, free of Venice and its doge yet close to Venetian interests. He brought in the Latin Church and barred the Orthodox from high office, but left Greek churches and clergy largely in peace, and his people seem content to go on as before under new lords. He has just finished the Kastro on Naxos and begun a cathedral. He has heard tales of Polyaigos's riches and envies them.
neighbours.secrets: His younger brother Pietro, whom he never felt easy with and often wonders about, is Satabus of Verditius, now at Polyaigos. Caterina da Vigonovo has met him as a wealthy noblewoman and is preparing a quiet bargain.

neighbours.name: Lordship of Negroponte
neighbours.summary: Euboea, sparsely peopled since William of Sicily's sack of 1157, fell after 1204 to three barons of Verona, the Triarchy, who made it a lordship of baronies named for Negroponte, the Venetian name for Chalkis's bridge, the city and then the whole island: the central barony at Chalkis, the northern at Oreoi, the southern at Karystos. Ravano dalle Carceri, one of the three, took the whole island and, defying his homeland, accepted Venice as overlord. After he died in 1216 the Venetian bailiffs halved each barony and shared the six among his kin and heirs. Aegaea lies under the sea not far off its coast (Euboea itself is described with Greece).
neighbours.ruler: The heirs of Ravano dalle Carceri, under Venetian bailiffs

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Candia
neighbours.summary: Venice's Candia, set up in 1212 once the republic had wrested the island from the Genoese pirate Enrico Pescatore; Boniface of Montferrat had sold it to the doge for 1000 marks. Four Venetian dukes have ruled it in turn for two years each, and Venetian families are encouraged to settle. The Greeks resent the higher taxes and tolls of the ports, and the mood is rebellious. The rulers are walling Chandax anew and building a harbour fortress, and they offer a handsome reward for the capture or death of Talos, the bronze 'demon' who sinks their ships.
neighbours.ruler: A Venetian duke, named for two years

neighbours.name: Venetian Lemnos
neighbours.summary: Lemnos, the only northern island Venice claimed in 1204, has been under Venetian rule since, and its new masters have claimed the whole island and its goods, the Lemnian Earth of Hephaistia above all, cutting into Ingasia's finances. Some magi read the choice as a sign of a secret deal between House Verditius and the old doge. The book names no governor; history has the Venetian Filocalo Navigajoso holding the island as a fief, with the title of megadux.

neighbours.name: Despotate of Rodos
neighbours.summary: Leo Gavalas, a rich and corrupt dynatos who came from Constantinople soon after it fell, has made himself despot of Rodos, an island Venice claims and where it has kept a naval base since 1082. He fears that free reading will make his subjects rebel, so one of his first acts was to confiscate every book; only works he has approved, which show him in a good light, may be sold.
neighbours.secrets: His closest adviser, an infernal hedge wizard, steers him, wrote the island's only books (a perverted Bible among them), and is gathering all its vis for himself.

neighbours.name: Monastery of St John the Divine, Patmos
neighbours.summary: Founded at the end of the eleventh century and later fortified against pirates and petty despots, the only house on holy Patmos, thronged with pilgrims. Its patron saint is St Leontios, a holy fool made a saint for his asceticism alone (see the Divine landscape). Some of its monks claim visions in the Cave of the Apocalypse.

neighbours.name: Nea Moni, Khios
neighbours.summary: The 'new monastery' of Khios, founded by the emperor Constantine IX, one of the largest in the old Byzantine Empire.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Chandax
neighbours.summary: Chandax, seat of the Kingdom of Candia, is also an archbishop's see; the book says no more of its clergy.

neighbours.name: The new cathedral of Naxos
neighbours.summary: The Latin cathedral Marco Sanudo has just begun beside his Kastro, as he brings the Western Church to the Cyclades while leaving the Orthodox churches largely alone.

neighbours.name: The church of Kos
neighbours.summary: The town church where the wreath from the Tree of Hippocrates hangs among the icons for a year after it is blessed, before the women carry it to the sea.

neighbours.name: Chandax
neighbours.summary: The chief city of Candia and the largest of the Greek islands, which the Venetians just call Candia, on the site of old Iraklion halfway along the north coast. The Saracens refounded it in the ninth century, ringed it with a moat and raided Byzantine shipping from it; the Byzantines razed and rebuilt it when they took it. Now seat of the kingdom and an archbishopric, it is getting a stronger wall over the Saracen defences and a new harbour fort. Mount Zeus's profile looms behind it.

neighbours.name: Rodos
neighbours.summary: The walled city at the north of the island, split by the Saracens into quarters, one still largely Jewish, with its own quarter for the rulers; a Venetian naval base since 1082, and now the despot's seat, where only books he approves may be sold.

neighbours.name: Naxos
neighbours.summary: The duke's seat, under the new Kastro, with a cathedral rising.

neighbours.name: Kos
neighbours.summary: A busy port among rich farms, round the Tree of Hippocrates, inside a Divine aura.

neighbours.name: Andros
neighbours.summary: The Cyclades' other great port, famous for its shipwrights; home port of Favonius and Memnos's yard.

neighbours.name: Myrina
neighbours.summary: One of the two largest towns of Lemnos, on its west coast.

neighbours.name: Hephaistia
neighbours.summary: The other great town of Lemnos, on the north-east coast, near the pits of the Lemnian Earth that Venice has taken over.

neighbours.name: Mytilene
neighbours.summary: The first of the five towns of Lesbos named for King Makaras's daughters, on an island where women rule.

neighbours.name: Antissa
neighbours.summary: A town of western Lesbos, birthplace of the minstrel Terpander, near Orpheus's grove of Orphykia.

neighbours.name: The Pirates of the Aegean
neighbours.summary: The countless crews who have raided the Archipelago since antiquity, now swollen in number by the empire's fall; some of their chiefs rule ports as despots. On the poor islets raiding is a respectable living. Lords hang them, but rulers have long hired them too, and some Venetian captains will deal with any who prey on their rivals. The Tribunal bans covenants from attacking one another's ships, but pirates know nothing of the Order, and robbing mundanes is not forbidden, only frowned on. They may be villains holding a covenant's people for ransom, or bold rogues standing up to greedy lords and captains.

details.wants: Booty and ransoms
details.offers: Hire as mercenaries; news of shipping

neighbours.name: Peter Monocheiros's crew
neighbours.summary: Peter 'One Hand', a pirate who sails with Favonius in two ships of his own, with eight of the covenant's best fighters sworn to him. He owes his life to Aeliophanes and is utterly loyal.

details.wants: Plunder, under Favonius's protection
details.offers: A third of the plunder to Favonius; eight capable warriors

neighbours.secrets: He gives the covenant a third of his plunder for the fleet's protection, passing anything identifiable to Basil to sell in far ports; his men wear masks at work and his ships are enchanted to change their look, so nothing leads back to Favonius.

neighbours.name: The trading house of Basil of Andros
neighbours.summary: Favonius's chief companion, captain of the Procne and a merchant-adventurer (City & Guild) well on his way to founding his own house; he keeps the fleet supplied, and his hot temper keeps him arguing with Verecunda over profit and adventure.

details.wants: Profitable voyages, and a trading house of his own
details.offers: Supplies, trade, sales in distant ports

neighbours.name: Constantinople
neighbours.summary:
The Queen of Cities: New Rome, raised by Constantine the Great on old Byzantium in 330, on a triangle of seven hills between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, and enriched by every emperor after him, by none more than Justinian. Roman to the bone, it is a city of forums, colonnades, baths, palaces, churches and monasteries, and it keeps its hippodrome, its senate house, its aqueduct and its slave market. In 1220 it is a filthy, dangerous shadow of itself: about a third still lies burnt and broken from the siege and the fires of 1203 and 1204, its people number fewer than 200,000 where Justinian ruled nearly half a million, and the rich live wall to wall with the destitute. The Latin conquerors have shipped most of its relics and treasures west and spend more effort stripping it than mending it. Civil order has gone: each of its many peoples mistrusts the others and protects itself with street gangs or hired soldiers.

Auras. Every place in the city lies in some aura, and each waxes and wanes with the calendar. The old gods' worship first left Faerie auras; Constantine's churches spread Divine ones that swallowed most of them; the city's many massacres, from the Nika riots to the sack of 1204, left Infernal patches that the weakened Dominion has not yet worn away. Magic auras were always few, most with preternatural tethers, and Jerbiton magi kept them alive by working magic in them every year; that has stopped since the conquest, so they are no longer tended. Most Divine auras here are Dominion, centred on an altar and as strong as the faithful who worship there, and so weaker than they were; the one relic left that could raise an empyreal aura is the Crown of Thorns, in the Venetian Quarter. Auras spread until they meet one as strong; where two of equal strength meet they simply touch, so a single step can lead from a Divine aura into an Infernal one.

The broken wards. Constantine walked the city's bounds behind a plough, binding its spirits in a Sol Invictus invocation that Justinian later carried out to the new walls. Two level 50 effects came of it: God's City lowered the Might of every Faerie and Infernal being inside the walls by 10 (Penetration 20), and the Walls of the City of God gave anyone storming them three extra botch dice. Both have lain dead since 1204, when someone took the palladium from a sealed vault beneath the Column of Constantine, together with other relics. No one knows what the palladium looks like, where it is or who took it; put it and the relics back and the wards would wake. The great riots that shaped the city's history have also ceased since the fall, which some think a side effect of the bindings.

The Order. Before the conquest the city held three covenants: Thermakopolis was wiped out, Moero's Garden fled to Nicaea with the Greek nobility, and Xylinites shut its gates. In 1220 two covenants of the Propontian phyle lie inside the walls, Michael's Tabula in the catacombs and the Criamon Clutch of Xylinites under an orphanage, while Passara of Verditius tends the automata of the Magnaura. Young Jerbiton magi above all want a covenant replanted in the city, and the Tribunal has not decided whether to encourage it; the site of Thermakopolis is the obvious place. Visiting magi rest and meet at the Baths of Zeuxippus.

Vis in the city (each described in its place): the Medusas' Tears in the Basilica Cistern (8 pawns of Imaginem at the summer solstice), the Serpent Column in the Hippodrome (8 pawns of Animal, by a rite of ram's blood that Moero's Garden found), and a few unnamed sources in the catacombs that Michael's Tabula has found. The book does not say whether any of them is one of the polity's common sources.

The most exact copy of the Synaxarion, the Orthodox calendar of more than two thousand saints with a short life and readings for each, compiled in the eleventh century and kept up to date, is here beside the Church of St John the Baptist. It lists saints the West does not, among them both Justinians and the patriarchs Photios and Ignatios.

Saints: Euphemia, the city's first official saint and its patron (an area saint, Divine Might 50), under the Theotokos, its protector; Cosmas and Damian, the unmercenary physician twins, saints of doctors and the suburbs (local, Divine Might 25). The greater saints (Divine Might 75) most invoked are St George and St John Chrysostom, and St Nicholas of Myra (area) for sailors, merchants, students and children. Oaths are sworn by St Basil of Caesarea or Saints Theodoros and Theophanes, who may punish a notorious perjurer; islanders swear by their river, after the Styx.
neighbours.secrets:
Three demons have long taken a close interest in the city: Golab, called the Seraphim's Foe, with Hulikang and Nike under him, who for centuries each ran one of the circus factions, the Greens and the Blues, and through them much of its politics and trade, despite the wards. Some suspect they now drive the 'Frank' and 'Venetian' factions; the book leaves it open, and the stilled riots may be their doing rather than the wards'.

The prince of Hell Akgah, who orchestrated the fall, has his lair in an Infernal regio about a dozen miles outside the walls (see the realms' places), and fought the Hagka in the Hippodrome in 1204.

neighbours.name: The Harbours of Constantinople
neighbours.summary:
Most visitors come by sea, and harbours line both the northern and southern sea walls, each behind its own outworks and towers. On the Marmara side lie the busy Harbour of Theodosius, midway along the southern wall, where ships from every corner of Mythic Europe put in and where a party arriving by ship most likely lands; the Kontoskalion, where the shrunken imperial navy rides at anchor under Latin command; and the Harbour of Julian below the imperial palaces, once kept for the court. On the Golden Horn the two busiest ports, the Neorion and the Prosphorion, were given to the Venetians for their warships and merchantmen.

From the quays the city's ruin is hard to see: merchantmen come in every day, boats ferry knights over the Bosporus, armed galleys hunt pirates and escort shipping, fishermen and dockers work without pause, and the conquerors keep the sea walls (thirty feet on the Golden Horn, forty-five on the Marmara, with hundreds of towers) in good repair. With so many soldiers about, the harbours are fairly safe.

neighbours.name: The Walls of Theodosius
neighbours.summary:
The land walls, never yet breached, running from the Golden Horn to the Sea of Marmara behind a ditch built in sections that can be flooded one by one: an outer wall thirty feet high and seven thick, a raised terrace (the peribolos), then an inner wall forty feet high and some seventeen thick, with nearly a hundred towers; the strip between ditch and outer wall, the patateichion, is raised too. With the sea walls they close the city in completely. Of the ten great gates, five serve travellers and five the army, with smaller posterns between.

The Golden Gate, a triumphal arch plated in gold between two great copper elephants, opened only for an emperor coming home victorious; it last swung open when Alexios V Murzuphlus slipped out through it by night after the crusaders took the walls. Further north, the gate of the Golden Mantle leads to Blachernae; it is crowned by a golden globe bearing a figure wrapped in a cloak, and legend says lightning will spare the city while the globe stays up. Folk think it ancient Greek work.

Getting in is easy: travellers and traders pass the gates by day, and enough hidden ways exist for a small party to slip in after dark. Moero's Garden knows a secret passage under the walls near the Gate of Pege, which its search parties use to come hunting for lost treasures and relics.
neighbours.secrets: The globe of the Golden Mantle may be one of the protective enchantments Hermetic magi made for the city, and one that failed.

neighbours.name: Porphyrio's Lair
neighbours.summary:
Somewhere under the waters off the city lies the lair of Porphyrio, the giant whale that wrecked ships in harbour and along the strait for months until Belisarius, with one galley and a hundred sailors, fought it from dawn to sunset; bristling with spears and burnt by Greek fire, it sank, and was not seen for generations. It still surfaces near the city now and then, without pattern, and has never attacked a ship since, but its coming foretells disaster: it was last sighted in April 1203, a week before the Venetian fleet filled the Sea of Marmara.

Theban magi, especially students of Hermetic divination, hold it to be a magical beast with a lair on the sea floor. Every search, even with Alexandria's glass submarine, has failed, and the current guess is that the lair lies in a Magic regio. The book gives the whale no stat block.

neighbours.name: The Forum of Constantine
neighbours.summary:
The most famous of the city's open plazas, on the crown of the Second Hill, ringed by colonnades and porticoes at the gateway to the imperial quarter. It is one of the great daily markets, and its trade includes the slave markets and the brothels; the Mese, the colonnaded Middle Way, runs through it from the Philadelpheion crossroads on the Third Hill down to the palaces, linking every forum of the city. Its column carried a statue of Constantine until a storm destroyed it, and a cross has stood there since early in the twelfth century.

Beneath the Column of Constantine lies a sealed underground vault, now empty, where the palladium at the heart of Constantine's wards was kept with other relics: the twelve baskets of the feeding of the five thousand, the axe Noah built the Ark with, the Magdalene's jar of perfume and the crosses of the two thieves. All went missing in 1204.
neighbours.secrets: Whoever restores the palladium and those relics to the vault wakes both of the city's wards again.

neighbours.name: The Column of Theodosius
neighbours.summary:
The heart of the Forum of Theodosius, also called the Forum Tauri, near the city's centre, where the butchers and fishmongers keep their stalls: a marble column 150 feet high with a spiral stair inside to a platform at the top. Its sides are carved with the Sibyl's prophecies in strange pictures and signs that make sense only once the event has come, the recent siege among them; Alexios V Murzuphlus was thrown from its top after his capture, and his death is carved on it too.

It stands in a Magic aura of 5, the strongest and largest in the city, filling the forum to its edges; no neighbouring aura comes near it, so it never rises or falls. Magi have dreamt of a covenant here, but the place is too public and the aura stops at the buildings round it.

Anyone who gazes at the carvings for an hour has a vision of things to come, as the Visions Flaw; only those with Premonitions can hope to read it (Intelligence + Premonitions against an Ease Factor the storyguide sets, 12 to begin with), and one who does gains some benefit when the event arrives, say +3 to a few rolls. The column is also a study source for Premonitions of Source Quality 6: it is built of six porphyry drums between iron bands, each good for one season's study, the top four reachable only by ladder or magic, in a crowded, distracting square (the windowless stair is no help).

neighbours.name: The Basilica Cistern
neighbours.summary:
A vast reservoir beneath the First Hill feeding the imperial quarter, its roof held up by 336 columns. It is one node in a maze of tunnels and chambers that runs to the Great Palace and to other rooms under the city. Water still reaches it through the Aqueduct of Valens, unrepaired for half a century, and the great open cisterns on the Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Hills, basins ringed with columns.

The Medusas' Tears. In the north-western corner two columns rest on stone medusa heads, brought from far away under Justinian, one set upside down and one on its side. If the water has covered them all year, the moss round their eyes can be scraped off at the summer solstice as 8 pawns of Imaginem vis. Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: The Venetian Quarter
neighbours.summary:
The home of the Republic of Venice's officials and people in the city, walled off from the rest between 1205 and 1207 and patrolled by Venetian soldiers, with its own ports on the Golden Horn. Inside it is a hive of trade; most feel safe, but many Greeks hate the merchants' exemptions, which shut them out of the shipping trade, and mistrust runs between Venetians, the other crusaders and the Greeks. Life is harder for ordinary Venetians than for their officials: much of the quarter is still ash and rubble, home to armed gangs and bandits, and smugglers prize it as the easiest way into the city.

Here, locked away, lies the Crown of Thorns: the Latin emperor's, pledged to the doge against a loan of 13,134 Mythic pounds, and never yet taken from the city. Entire, the crown has Faith 7 and the saintly powers Cure Blindness, Strengthen the Cripple and Mass Healing; each of its thorns is a relic in its own right. It is the one relic left in Constantinople strong enough to raise an empyreal aura.

Relic: the Crown of Thorns (Faith 7; Cure Blindness, Strengthen the Cripple and Mass Healing), whose every thorn is a Minor relic. It is the Latin emperor's, but the doge holds it as pledge for a loan of 13,134 pounds, locked away here in the Venetian quarter; it is the only relic left that can raise an empyreal aura in the city.

neighbours.name: The Baths of Zeuxippus
neighbours.summary:
A great bathhouse over a former temple of Zeus, adorned with more than eighty statues of famous Greeks and Romans and of the old gods, linked by passages to the Great Palace. It has been closed to the public since the Nika revolt of 532: some parts admit only nobles, others are given over to the army, and a former bathing hall serves as a prison, all far enough apart to keep bathers from prisoners. Near it, the old Temple of Aphrodite, made a royal stable late in the fourth century, still stands.

The Jerbiton magi of the city met here so often that they jokingly called themselves the Covenant of the Baths of Zeuxippus. Theban magi know there was never such a covenant, but the joke has grown into a rumour that magi of far Tribunals still believe. Unpopular with the townsfolk, the baths give visiting magi a quiet place to rest, and they are the unofficial meeting place of magi and their associates.

neighbours.name: The Lost Julian Library
neighbours.summary:
The library Julian the Apostate built late in the fourth century, said to have held over 600,000 texts: his own books and copies of every learned and literary work his scholars could find, with many curiosities, some magical. The most famous was the Iliad and the Odyssey written in gold on a dragon's gut thirty-seven yards long, which is said to make its reader wiser.

The building is long gone under later ones, and Julian's followers hid the collection after his death. Seekers of the Tribunal hunt it constantly and turn up lost sections now and then; the finest pieces are still hidden, and the competition for them is fierce.

neighbours.name: The Old House of Moero's Garden
neighbours.summary:
The site in the older part of the city that Ionnia of Jerbiton identified in 1163 as the home of the poetess Moero, of about 300 BC, lying in one of the city's few lacunae; there she founded Moero's Garden, with Moero's summoned ghost as its patron. The covenant fled to Nicaea after the conquest, leaving most of its library and collections behind, and its magi long to return.

Moero's ghost is still bound here, which is why Ionnia had to bind Hipparchus as the covenant's patron at Nicaea: the Tribunal requires a covenant's patron to live inside it. The covenant's search parties slip in through the passage near the Gate of Pege.

neighbours.name: The Hippodrome
neighbours.summary:
The heart of the city, 1,600 feet long and 400 wide, its straight northern end joined to the Great Palace and kept for the imperial family, its southern end curved; at its height it seated 80,000. Jousts have taken the place of chariot races, but jugglers, dancers, beast-tamers and tumblers still perform, and festivals, holy days and imperial ceremonies are held here. The statues that lined its arcades, Athena, an eagle on a serpent, Helen of Troy, the wolf with Romulus and Remus, a hippopotamus with a crocodile in its jaws, are mostly destroyed, torn down for their inlaid metal or from spite; townsfolk say many of them could move, sing, play music or act out a scene. Down the middle runs the spina, the stone pier the chariots raced round, with two great monuments left: the Serpent Column at the south and the Egyptian Obelisk at the north.

By day a Dominion aura of 1 surrounds stronger pockets: Faerie 2 round the Serpent Column, Magic 2 round the obelisk, and Infernal 2 in patches along the old track where the Nika fighting was worst and where the Bogomil leader Basil was burnt.

The ghosts of the Nika riots. Justinian lured the rioting Greens and Blues into the Hippodrome, and Belisarius cut down 30,000 of them. Every 14 January, at night, hundreds of Infernal ghosts rise from the ground here crying 'Nika!' (Victory). The city's Dominion once held them inside; it is weaker now, and they roam the Great Palace and the streets.

The automata of Ollaferus. Almost a third of the Hippodrome's statues were once automata by Ollaferus of Verditius, a second-generation magus who perfected the inner Mystery of automata for Verditius himself; each could play out one scene from Roman or Byzantine history or legend. Most have been smashed, melted or carried off. Verditius magi of the Tribunal want the few left, to decorate their workshops rather than to study, and pay others to haul half a ton of stone for them: a novice with a shard may be offered a token to neutralise it for delivering one.
neighbours.secrets: In 1204 the demon Akgah fought the Hagka here among the statues; the battle wrecked part of the arena, Akgah won, and the wounded Hagka fled. Crusaders who saw it took it for a vision of the lion of Venice triumphant.

neighbours.name: The Serpent Column
neighbours.summary:
Three twisted bronze serpents rising to hold a bronze bowl between their heads, at the southern end of the spina. It first stood in Apollo's temple at Delphi; Constantine brought it to the porch of Hagia Sophia and then here. An ancient ritual older than Hermetic theory, meant to keep snakes out of Apollo's temple, now works like a ward over the whole city: no mundane snake can enter it, though snakes with a Might pay it no heed.

Vis. Moero's Garden learnt that if a ram is sacrificed and its blood poured into the bowl at each solstice and equinox, the column drinks it; after the fourth offering, at the summer solstice, the blood comes back as a dark red clot worth 8 pawns of Animal vis.

The Faerie aura of 2 comes from the faerie in the regio above the column, who calls himself Belisarius (see the Bestiary). Its level, Faerie 4, is the Hippodrome as it was; there he leads a little band of urban faeries in an endless staging of the riots' last battle, his imperial guard against the mob, as a lesson that rightful rule and tradition must win over change. He needs a human audience and sends his followers into the city to lure people in.

levels.name: Belisarius's Hippodrome
levels.enter: Walk round the column widdershins holding a sword of Roman make.
levels.notes: A regio as large as the Hippodrome, showing it in all its ancient splendour, where Belisarius's urban faeries replay the end of the Nika riots.

links.note: the faerie of the Serpent Column's regio

neighbours.name: The Egyptian Obelisk
neighbours.summary:
Set up at the northern end of the spina by Julian the Apostate, who fetched it from Egyptian Thebes as part of his campaign to revive the old gods. It broke on the journey: of its ninety feet only the top thirty survive, covered in hieroglyphs and in carvings of the Hippodrome's Roman spectacles. A Magic aura of 2 surrounds it.

Its carvings can be read as a riddle of the future: Intelligence + Magic Lore + a stress die against an Ease Factor of 15, handled as Hermetic divination; since it is older than the Order, its visions may break the Lesser Limit of Time. Each of the two lost thirds, if found, lowers the Ease Factor by 3, to 9 for the whole stone, but there are few clues to where they are.

neighbours.name: The Great Palace
neighbours.summary:
The larger of the two imperial palaces, in the south-east overlooking the Sea of Marmara, adorned and extended throughout the city's history until it is really five: the Chalke, the Magnaura, the Daphne, the Sacred Palace and the Bucoleon, joined by passages and walks that also lead to the Hippodrome and the Baths of Zeuxippus. Like Blachernae it is a sprawl of fortified stone buildings full of riches, guarded day and night, and few are let in. Some thirty chapels belong to it, among them the Virgin of the Pharos. The palace schools of the Magnaura are among the most famous in the city.

Relic: the Holy Lance, the pilum of the centurion Longinus, in the city since the eighth century and now in the Latin emperor's palace (Faith 3, Expel Demons; a Powerful Relic). A second, longer lance found at Antioch in 1098 seems genuine too.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Bucoleon
neighbours.summary:
On the slope of the First Hill above the Marmara harbours, the home of the early emperors, close to the Hippodrome, Hagia Sophia and the Mese and riddled with secret passages under them. Under the Angeloi it housed favoured courtiers, the imperial kin and the empress. Baldwin of Flanders took it in 1204, and it has been the residence of the Latin emperors ever since; it stands empty of its master in 1220, awaiting Robert of Courtenay.

The Holy Lance of Longinus, in the city since the eighth century, lies in the Latin emperor's palace: a Roman pilum of Faith 3 whose saintly power is to Expel Demons.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Magnaura
neighbours.summary:
A huge palace whose name means 'fresh breeze', with many suites and a throne room for receiving honoured guests. Its marvels all still work: a golden throne that rises to the ceiling at a word, two gilded lions before it that open their jaws to roar and lash their tails, and a gilded bronze tree whose jewelled birds of precious metal sing. While visitors lay prostrate before the emperor, the throne rose, the lions roared and the birds sang together.

The automata were made early in the tenth century by Aella of Verditius, a Cretan, who worked closer to the emperors than many liked and was charged several times with being a court wizard; her husband, Vaanes of Guernicus, defended her, and she was never convicted, though she was ostracised twice and came back both times to tend her works. Her heir in that duty, Passara of Verditius, keeps them from decay in 1220 and lives in apartments here given to her by the emperor's autocrat.
neighbours.secrets: Whether Passara serves the Latin emperor, as Formosos of Guernicus insists, the book leaves to the storyguide.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Blachernae
neighbours.summary: The smaller, newer imperial palace in the north-west corner of the city, on the Sixth Hill above the Golden Horn near the sea walls; built in the fifth and sixth centuries outside the walls, it was enclosed in 627 and became the favourite residence of the last Greek emperors, and their prison too: Isaac II Angelos was shut in one of its towers when his brother Alexios III overthrew him. Many old imperial crowns kept here were carried off in the three days of looting. That plunder and the notorious habits of the Angeloi, its last residents, have given the whole complex an Infernal aura of 2. The gate of the Golden Mantle leads to it.

neighbours.name: The Porphyry Chamber
neighbours.summary:
The imperial birthing room, walled in purple porphyry that Egypt sent in the fourth century and draped in purple silk; the book does not say in which palace it lies. A child born there to a reigning emperor and empress is porphyrogennetos, 'born in the purple', and outranks elder siblings born before the accession, even as a girl: Empress Zoe was crowned over male rivals on that claim. Such princesses may not marry outside the empire, though that rule has been broken, to ruin. Being born in the purple brings a claim to the throne, a good education and the people's love, and so many such children have been blinded or shut in convents and monasteries when their parents fell; with emperors changing so fast, several living people can claim the rank. The Latins honour the custom but loosely, and the room is no longer always guarded.

Porphyrogenitos. A character born in the chamber gains a Supernatural Virtue at birth, free of the usual allowance, and because of the city's shifting auras it need not be Divine: on a simple die, 1 Infernal, 2 Magic, 3 or 4 Faerie, 5 to 9 Divine, and 10 a Major Virtue in place of the Minor (roll the realm again, ignoring another 10). Others assume the gift is God's blessing, as the emperors say; its true realm may stay hidden even from its bearer.

neighbours.name: Hagia Sophia
neighbours.summary:
The Church of the Holy Wisdom, the Great Church: the third church on its site and each bigger than the last, a basilica whose great dome, 168 feet above the floor and carried on columns, makes it seem round; it is the largest cathedral in Mythic Europe. It was stripped in the sack: its relics taken, its high altar broken up for the gold, its chandeliers torn down for the silver, and orgies of lust and slaughter in the three days of looting fouled its Divine aura. Worse to the Greeks, it has passed from the Orthodox to the Latin rite under a Latin patriarch who answers to the pope. Emperors are still crowned here, in ceremonies little changed from the Greek ones.

Auras. The rebuilt high altar, a poor copy of the old, centres a Dominion aura of 5; the aisles and the outer porticoes have a Dominion aura of 2. The nave holds an Infernal aura of 7, left by the crusaders' massacre of more than a thousand innocents there, and with most of the relics gone the Dominion is too weak to wear it down.

Relics too heavy to carry off still work. The Column of St. Gregory the Thaumaturge, one of the dome's supports, gives +6 to Recovery rolls and heals a wound one step faster (a Heavy Wound in a Medium Wound's time, a Light Wound in a day). On one of the nine doors from the narthex into the nave hangs a tube: a sick man who sets it to his lips has his illness drawn out of him.

Its architects were Isidore of Miletus and the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles, who gathered columns from across the empire, those of Ephesus's Temple of Artemis among them. They quarrelled, Isidore wanting refinements drawn from Heron of Alexandria, and he had his way when Anthemius died within the year, of natural causes, it was said, though rumour doubted it. Theban magi, Catella of Alexandria above all, would like to study the building for Heron's ideas: a season of daily study would uncover them, and Catella will pay any magus with a workable plan in vis and gold for his time and notes.

Relics: fragments of the True Cross, found by St Helena near Jerusalem, were kept here in numbers; the Venetians and Latins now hold them, and the exiles carried many small ones to Nicaea. A piece as long as a man's leg has Faith 10 (Divine Might 100) and heals any wound at once; a hand-sized piece Faith 3, healing a Medium Wound; a sliver Faith 1, an ordinary relic. Tiny ones are common, worn in gold reliquaries, and the Cross never runs out of them. The Image of Edessa came here from Jerusalem in 944 and the Crown of Thorns in 1063; the Mandylion, the first icon not made by hands, was stolen in the sack.
neighbours.secrets: The insights from Heron are really there in the building's fabric, for a magus who spends the season.

neighbours.name: The Crypts of the Holy Apostles
neighbours.summary:
The crypts under the Church of the Holy Apostles, burial place of emperors and patriarchs until 1028, now looted by men who dug up the emperors for their crowns and jewels. By day the church's Dominion aura of 4 keeps down an Infernal aura of 3 rising from the crypts; at night the Dominion falls to 3 and the Infernal rises to 4, taking the church over and letting the thing below roam it.

That thing is Zeno, emperor from 474 to 491: once Tarasicodissa, a mercenary chief of the Isaurians from the Taurus Mountains, hated, plotted against, overthrown and buried alive here, begging for mercy for three days before he fell silent. He never died. Demon-blooded, he needs no food or air and does not age; Leo Grammaticus painted him as shaggy, misshapen, goat-footed, hairy-legged, black of skin and absurdly built. Each night he climbs out of his open sarcophagus to prowl the church, but he cannot live outside an Infernal aura, so he can hardly leave it, and he kills and eats anyone he catches. The book gives him no stat block.

Hermetic legend says city magi once hid occult books and papers in the crypts, trusting the ghosts of the emperors to guard them, and necromancers called up the ghosts of emperors not gone to Heaven in the Infernal aura of Zeno's lair. Both were perilous.
neighbours.secrets: The storyguide may hide almost any treasure here, perhaps a clue to another story, to be won only by getting past Zeno.

neighbours.name: Latin Emperor of Constantinople
neighbours.summary:
The emperor of Romania, as the crusaders call the empire they made in 1204. By their pact with Venice he holds a quarter of the old empire directly, while the Venetians and the other crusade lords take three-eighths each; under him come the vassalli, the Frankish barons and the Greek lords of simple homage who accepted the new order, among them the King of Thessaloniki, the Prince of Achaea and his barons, the Duke of Athens and the Duke of Naxos. His court is his private council of trusted men and the council of the empire, which joins him, the Venetian podestà with his council, and the Frankish barons; the old Byzantine bureaucracy runs on beneath, since taxes, courts and supplies still need clerks.

Its emperors have not lasted. A college of six Venetians and six crusaders chose Baldwin of Flanders over Boniface of Montferrat; Baldwin was taken by the Bulgarians at Adrianople in 1205 and died in captivity. His brother Henry, crowned in August 1205, held the shrunken realm together until his sudden death in 1216, perhaps poisoned by his Bulgarian wife Maria, who fled. Peter of Courtenay, elected next, was seized by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epiros on his way from Durazzo in 1217 and is thought to have died his prisoner. His widow Yolanda reached the city by sea and ruled as regent from 1217 to 1219, making peace with Bulgaria and Nicaea and marrying her daughter Marie to the Nicene emperor. After her sudden death the throne went to her elder son Philip of Namur, who refused it; his brother Robert has accepted but will not reach the city until 1221.

So the empire is leaderless in 1220, a narrow strip round its capital, and at war again: Nicaea has just broken three years of peace, and the outlook is poor. The emperor still owns the Crown of Thorns, though it is pledged to the doge, and the Holy Lance lies in his palace.

The book leaves the throne simply empty; history has the barons governing through regents, Conon de Béthune until his death late in 1219 and then the papal legate Giovanni Colonna.
neighbours.secrets: Some say Baldwin was seen alive in Flanders, and House Tremere is whispered to know more of his fate than it says; the indiscreet Redcap who spread that tale died soon after in a fall from his horse, and the magistrates of the day let it lie. Peter's body was never found either. Hermetic gossip ties the vanished Maria of Bulgaria to the Daughters of Erictho.

neighbours.name: Podestà of Romania
neighbours.summary: The governor Venice sends to rule its people and holdings in the east, kept on a short leash for fear the quarter breaks away from the republic. He deals with the Latin emperor, sits with his own council on the council of the empire, and runs the eastern Venetian possessions as he judges best, forever assuring Venice that its interests come first. The Venetian Council of Constantinople advises him, as the Council of Venice advises the doge, and both answer to the doge and that council in the end. The Venetian lands of western Greece are ruled straight from Venice, and Durazzo and Corfu are expressly outside his reach. He holds the Crown of Thorns in pledge for the doge. In 1220 the podestà is Ottaviano Quirino.

neighbours.name: The Latin Patriarchate of Constantinople
neighbours.summary:
Since the conquest the patriarch in Hagia Sophia has been a Latin under the pope, and the Orthodox Church in Constantinople is in theory subject to Rome; the Orthodox patriarch, Manuel I Charitopoulos, sits at Nicaea. Under the crusaders' pact Venice names the Latin patriarch: its man Thomas Morosini was the first, grudgingly accepted by Innocent III; the see stood empty from his death in 1211 until Gervase was appointed in 1215, and is empty again since Gervase died in 1219, the pope not yet having named a successor.

The Latin Church has set up new sees with Latin bishops over mostly Orthodox priests, seeks more Latin clergy from the West, and has brought the Latin rite into many churches. Some clergy have accepted the union; many who reject it still serve in the new hierarchy, and most of the people stay loyal to Orthodoxy, so an attempt to stop the procession of icons on the Feast of the Triumph of Orthodoxy means a riot.

relics.name: The Column of St. Gregory the Thaumaturge
The healing tube on the nave door

neighbours.name: Hagia Eirene
neighbours.summary: The Church of the Holy Peace, the Old Church, the oldest in the city: the third building on its site, rebuilt when Justinian rebuilt Hagia Sophia, a rectangle under a central dome with an outer atrium and narthex. It held few relics and so escaped the worst of the plunder. Dominion aura 4.

neighbours.name: The Church of the Virgin of the Pharos
neighbours.summary: The 'Holy Chapel' of the crusaders, one of the thirty chapels of the Great Palace, kept for the emperor and his family. It became an immense treasury of relics, and every one has gone: two pieces of the True Cross, the Holy Lance's iron point, the nails from Christ's hands, His blood in a phial of crystal, His tunic, the Crown of Thorns, part of the Virgin's robe and the head of St. John the Baptist. Dominion aura 4, falling to 3 at night.

neighbours.name: The Church of the Holy Apostles
neighbours.summary: A Greek cross under five domes, once the busiest church in the city and the burial place of emperors and patriarchs until Constantine VIII was laid here in 1028. Its relics were stolen, many of them to Venice: the heads of Andrew, Luke and Timothy, and the Column of the Flagellation, where Christ was bound to be scourged. Looters even dug up the emperors. Its Dominion aura of 4 falls to 3 at night, when the Infernal aura of the crypts below overcomes it.

neighbours.name: St. John the Baptist of Studius and the Studion
neighbours.summary: One of the city's most celebrated churches, founded by the Roman patrician Studius in 463, a plain basilica with nave, narthex and atrium, beside the Studion, the monastery whose stone buildings stand round a square and which is the intellectual heart of the empire. The church escaped the worst of the looting, perhaps because it gathered books rather than relics, and keeps a Dominion aura of 5. The Studion carries on as if the Latins were not there, and its library is the largest collection of church and secular books in either the Latin or the Byzantine Empire.

neighbours.name: The Monastery of St. Christopoulos
neighbours.summary:
A walled monastery of several acres inside the city walls, in a quarter mostly given to pasture and orchards, founded as a lavra of monks in cells in 823. Romanos III Argyros, Zoe's first husband, endowed it richly, founding in 1030 an orphanage and school paid for by the treasury and run by the monks, and in 1031 giving it a tiny, exquisite icon of a little-known saint, Loukia. Under a great golden icon of Christ Pantokrator over the gate lie a small vineyard, pastures and wide gardens; the basilica stands at the centre with the refectory, kitchen, laundry and bakehouse round it, and some thirty black clergy live in small wooden cell-houses scattered across the grounds. At the west end an ancient, roofless bathhouse keeps two baths, one a fishpond and one still used by the monks, with the infirmary and storehouses behind. At the east end are the guest quarters, the school and a hostel for sixty boys, the famous orphanage, with the master's house, the boys' refectory, a scriptorium and a library beside them.

The orphanage was long a source of eunuchs for the palace: paying families sent boys to learn music, and those whose voices suited were gelded for the choirs, while children too dangerous to the throne were sent here to be castrated. The Latins still fund it, but they find the practice disgusting and the demand has nearly gone. The monks know that holy hermits of extreme mortification live in the old cistern under the orphanage, and leave them alone.
neighbours.secrets: The hermits are the Criamon magi of Xylinites.

neighbours.name: The Church of St. John the Baptist at Hebdomon
neighbours.summary: The chief of the many churches of Hebdomon, seven miles out along the Egnatian Road, in the town where the early emperors were crowned before riding through the Golden Gate to the Hippodrome.

neighbours.name: The City of Constantinople
neighbours.summary: The capital of the Latin Empire and still the greatest market of Mythic Europe: goods from the whole world are sold here, and anything can be had for a price. Its people number under 200,000, a babel of tongues. The main streets run straight in the Roman way, and even the lanes are more ordered than in other cities; the Mese crosses the city from the Philadelpheion to the palaces. Most of the city is open to anyone brave enough, but some quarters are dangerous by day and all but the best-guarded buildings are deadly by night; the palaces are watched always, parish churches are always open, and the great churches are kept locked except for feasts and important visitors. The guilds trade where they always have: candle makers, goldsmiths, silversmiths and perfumers by the portico of Hagia Sophia, butchers and fishmongers in the Forum Tauri, cattle and horse dealers in the Forum Amastrianum, slaves and harlots in the Forum of Constantine.
neighbours.ruler: The Latin emperor, through the city's prefect

neighbours.name: Hebdomon
neighbours.summary: The largest town outside the walls, a middling city seven miles out on the European shore by the Egnatian Road to Rome. Once an imperial summer retreat, it grew into a naval port and a place of ceremony, where early emperors were crowned before processing through the Golden Gate to the Hippodrome. It has many churches, St. John the Baptist chief among them, a palace of Justinian, forums and monasteries; to the north lies the Campus, the plain where the army camped before campaigns. The round tower of the Cyclobion guards its harbour, a favourite landing for friend and foe alike, though the town itself has no walls; the crusaders first came ashore here. Its governor surrendered it to the Latins after the city fell, and they have held it since.

neighbours.name: Galata
neighbours.summary: A fortified town across the Golden Horn, for centuries one of the city's main defences. Its castle anchored the great chain that could be raised across the Horn to close the northern harbours, until the crusaders stormed it in June 1203 and broke the chain, a sign of what was coming. The crusaders lived here until April 1204, when they moved into the richer houses of the conquered city.

neighbours.name: The Guilds of Constantinople
neighbours.summary: The city's trades have been organised in guilds far longer than in the West, and some exist here that Paris or London would not see for generations. They range from the silk makers, almost noble, to caulkers and street sweepers little better than peasants. Unlike Western guilds struggling for freedom from the magistrates, all of them are arms of the state, and even the greatest guild master obeys the prefect. Each still lives and sells in its old quarter.

details.rules: Every guild is run by the state, under the city's prefect
details.wants: Their old trades, quarters and privileges kept
details.offers: Goods of every kind, craftsmen, market news

neighbours.name: The Gangs of Constantinople
neighbours.summary: With civil law gone since the conquest, every people of the city, Greek, Venetian, Frankish and the rest, guards its own with makeshift gangs or hired swords, and none trusts the others. Armed bands and bandits nest in the burnt-out ruins, the ash of the Venetian Quarter among them, and smugglers use the Venetian ports to slip goods in.

details.wants: Safety for their own people, and loot
details.offers: Protection, muscle, smuggling, a way in by night

neighbours.secrets: Some suspect the demons Hulikang and Nike, once patrons of the Greens and Blues, of now stirring up a 'Frank' and a 'Venetian' faction; the book does not say if it is true.

neighbours.name: The Venetian Council of Constantinople
neighbours.summary: The council that advises the podestà, on the model of the council that advises the doge; it and the podestà answer to the doge and the Council of Venice. Through the podestà it sits in the council of the empire.

details.wants: Venice's trade privileges kept and the quarter loyal
details.offers: Shipping, credit, the Golden Horn ports

neighbours.name: Belisarius's Urban Faeries
neighbours.summary: A small troupe of city faeries in the regio above the Serpent Column, led by the faerie who calls himself Belisarius. They act the last battle of the Nika riots over and over, the rioters against Belisarius and his guards, and go out into the city to lure mortals in to watch.

details.wants: Human watchers for their show

neighbours.name: The Mithraeum of Michael's Tabula
neighbours.summary:
A forgotten temple of Mithras under a ruined quarter of the city, in a Magic aura of 3, reached through the catacombs. The magi of Michael's Tabula have made it a rough council chamber, with the stone tablet of their oath laid on the old altar, and cut laboratories, some of them shared, in the chambers round it. New stone walls, raised with their patron's help, close every way in, and only a magus with one of the covenant's magical keys can pass them; trusted allies alone are brought below, and other visitors are met in the magi's houses in the city.

The covenant has found a few sources of vis in the catacombs; the book does not describe them.

neighbours.name: The Cistern of Xylinites
neighbours.summary:
A huge vaulted cistern under the orphanage and eastern grounds of the monastery of St. Christopoulos, partly drained in the eleventh century and still flooded. Six fine laboratories are cut into its walls, reachable only by the little boats moored at the foot of the stairs; hidden staircases lead down from locked rooms in the orphanage buildings, and the cistern passes for a storehouse. Flooded tunnels branch off carrying water across the city, a maze a boat can explore, and the magi use them to slip out unseen on business.

The icon of St. Loukia sits in a small shrine in an alcove still reachable only by boat. A Magic aura of 3 spreads from it in a perfect sphere wide enough to take in the orphanage and the eastern end of the monastery, and ends where it meets the Dominion over the middle and west of the grounds. The orphan boys tell tales of haunted storerooms and mad hermits below, and a few bold ones have broken curfew to explore the vaults.
neighbours.secrets: The aura flows from Loukia herself: she is not dead but held in something like Twilight between this world and the Magic Realm, and magic pours through her into the world.

neighbours.name: Anatolia
neighbours.summary:
Asia Minor, where East meets West: a great central plateau walled off from the coasts by two long mountain chains, the Taurus in the south and the Pontic range in the north. The emperors once ruled all of it in provinces, or themes, but since the twelfth century much has gone to the Seljuk Turks, and in 1220 the Greeks keep only the shores: the Aegean coast west of the Taurus and the Black Sea coast north of the Pontic mountains. The interior and the lands beyond are fought over by Turks, Persians, Pechenegs, Cumans and Georgians.

The Tribunal has always kept to Byzantine soil, so its covenants sit on the Aegean shore, round the Sea of Marmara and by the Black Sea. Theban magi once founded covenants on the far edges, nearer foreign wizards and strange magic, but every one of them has failed, from neglect, invasion or something stranger; the Byzantine magi of the plateau fled after Manzikert in 1071 and have never gone back. Two covenants remain on this shore: Alexandria above Smyrna, of the Kretan phyle, which takes in southern Nicaea, and Moero's Garden in Nicaea itself, of the Propontian phyle, which takes in the north.

Most of the Greek coast belongs to the Empire of Nicaea, which has just gone back to war with the Latins of Constantinople; the Latins hold the northern Troad and part of Bithynia, the Sultanate of Rum holds the plateau and Sinope, and the Empire of Trebizond holds the far end of the Black Sea.

Vis of Anatolia (each in its place): the clay votive limbs of the Asklepieion at Pergamos (12 Corpus a year), the old Dionysian vineyard on Mount Tmolus by Philadelphia (Mentem, distilled from its wine), the magical plants of Trebizond's gardens (several would give vis every year if harvested properly), and perhaps the time-slowed regio of the Seven Sleepers' cave near Ephesus. The book does not say which of them, if any, are the polity's common sources. The Great Altar of Pergamos powers ritual spells without vis, at a price.

Saint: Prokopios, the first martyr of Diocletian's persecution, much loved in Caesarea (local, Divine Might 25).

links.note: Alexandria's glass submarine, chained to a ship at Smyrna

neighbours.name: Bithynia
neighbours.summary:
The north-west corner of Anatolia, facing Constantinople and the Thracian shore across the Sea of Marmara: wide forests, green hills and rich valleys, famous for its oranges and other fruit and for its grain. It is full of old and great cities, and armies have tramped over it again and again these twenty years. It is the march between the Latin Empire and the Empire of Nicaea, and its coastal castles have changed hands many times.

Six years of peace followed Theodore Laskaris's treaty with the Latins, sealed in 1219 by his marriage to a niece of the late Emperor Henry; but in 1220 the emperor is massing troops along the border for a new attack, and the Bithynians watch them gather with dread.

neighbours.name: The Roads about Nicaea
neighbours.summary:
The highways outside Nicaea's walls, where lone travellers are now and then found torn to pieces, roughly once a month. Most townsfolk blame bandits or skirmishers from one army or the other; a few recall the tale of St Andrew the apostle, who drove off seven demons in the shape of slavering dogs that were killing wayfarers here, then raised from the dead a young man the same seven had savaged in his bed, who followed the saint from then on.

The seven still hunt the roads round the city, though they may not pass its walls: the Demons of Nicaea, see the Bestiary. They strike at dusk or just after, choose people travelling alone, leave large parties be, and flee a stronger band. A Redcap riding solo is just the prey they like.

links.note: seven demon dogs on the roads outside the walls

neighbours.secrets: No magus has yet connected the roadside killings with the demons; a Redcap of Alexandria or Moero's Garden's covenfolk on an errand are the likeliest next victims.

neighbours.name: The Warren beneath Nicomedia
neighbours.summary:
Nicomedia is shaken by an earthquake about once a century, which brings down houses and starts fires. Some Theban magi suspect an old titan lies bound under the city and strains at its chains every hundred years. The townsfolk would laugh at them: everyone knows it is the dragon St George the Megalomartyras (the 'great martyr') wounded long ago, writhing in agony in tunnels below the streets.

George, a Roman tribune from Cappadocia, wounded a dragon to save a king's daughter offered to it and led the beast back to the city on a leash; towns from Jerusalem to Ireland claim the tale, perhaps Nicomedia among them. Whatever the truth, something does lie under the city. The book gives it no aura or realm.

neighbours.name: The Troad
neighbours.summary:
The big peninsula of north-western Anatolia (Troas), with a cold, wet north on the Sea of Marmara and a milder west on the Aegean, hot in summer and dry inland. Seven rivers run off the plateau of Mount Ida through gorges to the sea, and the cliffs and small bays of the shore offer many sites for a town that wants defending.

As in Bithynia, Latin crusaders hold the northern half, quiet since the peace of 1216: their lords govern and let the people thrive, and many of their knights are away fighting the Bulgarians. Theodore Laskaris means to exploit their absence and march on Holkos on the Hellespont; at the saga's start his army is gathered and the blow is about to fall.

neighbours.name: The Hellespont
neighbours.summary:
The thirty-eight-mile strait between Greece and Anatolia that links the Aegean with the Sea of Marmara, called the straits of St George by the French; Greeks and Persians long used it as a moat and a frontier. Though only one to four miles across, it is hard sailing: its currents flow either way with the tide and the hour, and pilots steer with great care.

Holkos, the Latin port where the strait meets the Marmara, is Laskaris's goal; he would make it a second base for his navy, to guard the straits against Venetian shipping. History has him take it, and the Latins, beset from the north, ask for peace in 1221.

neighbours.name: The Vantage Point of Xerxes
neighbours.summary:
A small round hill near Abydos, west of Holkos along the shore, from which the whole Hellespont can be seen. Looked at closely it is man-made, worn by age and wind. Artabanos, the sorcerer of Xerxes, raised it in the Persian Wars and set a marble throne on top that sharpened the king's sight by magic; the throne is gone.

Whoever stands on the hill still sees the strait and its shores as if with Keen Vision. The hill has an Infernal aura of 3.

links.note: the demon bound beneath Xerxes's hill

neighbours.secrets: Artabanos made a druj build the hill in a single day, then bound her under it and fed her power into the king's view; her malice seeped through and filled Xerxes with doubt and gloom. She is bound there still (Infernal Might 30, an Obsession of Doubt; see the Bestiary), and anyone using the view is open to her Obsession.

neighbours.name: Ilion (Troy)
neighbours.summary:
Priam's city, Ilium to the Latins, razed by the Greeks at the end of the Trojan War, about 1184 BC by Eratosthenes's reckoning. Nothing stands on the sandy shore now, the Scamander has dried up, and even Augustus's Roman town has vanished without a stone. It matters nothing to Greeks or Turks as land, but much as propaganda: many Westerners claim Trojan descent and call the Latin conquest of Constantinople Troy's revenge on the Greeks.

Magi find it important and perilous. So many tales are told of Ilion that it might be called the cradle of storytelling, and it swarms with faeries each longing to replay a story. The beach and the stony field have a Faerie aura of 2, riddled with hidden Faerie regiones that overlap and connect in a bewildering maze. Merinita magi say one holds a faerie city called Ilion, reached only by sea, ever readying for the siege; others replay the Greek ships and camp, the bloody plain and the burning city. The strong faeries each take one scene from a hero's life, so there are several Akhilles, several Paris and several Odysseus.

Left alone, the faeries play their parts idly; a mortal visitor is chum in the water, and the mightiest snatch him for their own tales, the lesser ones pulling the other way. Several Hektors, say, will each want him in a different part of Hektor's story. The strongest can shut a regio and keep their captives fighting the war for ever, and locals say people who wander the plain of Troy can vanish for good and that the ghosts of the fallen haunt it.

Every few Tribunals someone proposes a covenant here. In 1109 the Tribunal let Droserius of Merinita and four others found Wilusa, claiming the spirit of the Scamander had promised to be its patron; by the next meeting it had vanished and no search found a trace. The Tribunal now turns down any new proposal with ease.

levels.name: Wilusa's Troy
levels.notes: The regio in which the covenant of Wilusa was raised in 1109, now dressed as Troy and closed by the faerie who calls himself Odysseus; time runs slow inside.

neighbours.secrets:
Wilusa was built swiftly by magic in a Faerie regio of aura 4, but not the one where the Scamander's spirit dwells: a faerie calling himself Odysseus fooled Droserius, then sealed the regio. He has glamoured the covenant to look like Troy and throws the war's last assault at it again and again, the magi defending it by reflex; by bending time, the faeries have kept it up for more than a century, while the magi think only months have passed. Odysseus is fully cognizant and hopes to gather enough vitality to change his own story.

Finding that regio is hard: other faeries lure searchers into their own tales, it takes good Faerie Lore and patient exploring, and more than one regio stages the sack, so beating the 'Greeks' may only show the searchers they are in the wrong Troy. Even rescued, Droserius and his sodales will be loath to leave until shown that a hundred years have gone by.

neighbours.name: The Acropolis of Pergamos
neighbours.summary:
A great city to the Greeks and early Romans that has long since dwindled: its old acropolis, a stair of terraces above the Caicus and its plain, is a jumble of Greek and Roman ruins. To Greeks of 1220 it matters as one of the seven churches of St John's Revelation; the Church of St John, raised over a temple of Isis and Serapis, serves the Christians who still live there.

To magi it matters for its temples, ruined and mostly unexplored: above all the Library of Pergamos, once the rival of Ptolemy's at Alexandria in Egypt. Pergamos took to parchment while Alexandria still wrote on papyrus, so Hermetic scholars hope codices survive in hidden rooms underground. Mark Antony gave most of its books to Cleopatra as a wedding gift, but Theban Seekers have turned up a few texts left behind.

neighbours.name: The Library of Pergamos
neighbours.summary: The ruined library on the upper acropolis, with a Magic aura of 2. Most of its scrolls went to Egypt with Cleopatra, but Seekers have found a few remaining texts, and secret rooms below may still hold parchment codices.

neighbours.name: The Temples of Dionysus and Athena at Pergamos
neighbours.summary: Two ruined temples on the upper acropolis, one to Dionysus and one, the Sanctuary of Athena Polias Nikephoros, to Athena the Bringer of Victory; each has a Faerie aura of 3.

neighbours.name: The Great Altar of Pergamos
neighbours.summary:
A huge open-air altar at the north of the acropolis, on a terrace above St John's basilica: about forty feet long, twenty deep and up to forty high, Ionic columns along three sides over four great friezes of the gods' war with the titans and the gods' family trees, and on the fourth side a long flight of steps up to the central podium. Christians shun it, for St John's Revelation calls it Satan's throne.

Magi know it has a Faerie aura of 4, and guess it was once a magic site too, as the friezes show the faerie gods beating the magical titans. Its oddity: a Hermetic magus who casts a ritual spell standing on it needs no vis, the altar supplying the power. The cost is that a botch is tainted as if by Faerie vis, and even a good casting may have strange side effects. The locals think it evil and have run off magi before as demon worshippers, so, with vis plentiful in the Tribunal, it is little used; but Lucian and his Children of Olympos think it central to their plan to make pacts with the Greek gods.

links.note: the titan bound under the great altar

neighbours.secrets:
The altar is the lock on the prison of Klymene, Titaness of fame (Magic Might 50, see the Bestiary), one of the titanesses who stayed neutral in the Titanomachy and were bound away from Tartaros. A quirk of her binding lets magi draw on her power for their rituals. The bonds have a strength of 50, restored at each new year, and each ritual cast here wears them down by the pawns it would normally cost; if they fall to nothing within one year, the altar splits in two and she goes free.

She thought her prison a kindness, gentler than Tartaros and shared with her sisters, and freed she has nowhere to go: she might go back to the Magic Realm, settle on a mountain of the Tribunal and upset all around her, or range the land freeing other titanesses to bring back their old revels.

neighbours.name: The Asklepieion of Pergamos
neighbours.summary: A sanctuary of Asklepios two miles south of the acropolis, built over a sacred healing spring. It began as an offshoot of the shrines at Epidauros and grew more famous in the second century through Galen of Pergamos, who studied and taught here and whose ideas still shape the medicine of 1220. It has a Magic aura of 3.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: 12 pawns of Corpus a year, as small clay body parts like the votive offerings of the sick. The book does not say who gathers them.

neighbours.name: Lydia
neighbours.summary:
Mountain country south of the Troad, its Aegean shore a run of cliffs, sandy coves, bays and good harbours. The Hermus, one of the great rivers of Asia Minor, crosses it from the Anatolian mountains to the Bay of Smyrna. A Byzantine province since the fourth century, it was briefly overrun by the Turks more than once in the twelfth. Legend makes it the homeland of the Amazons and the scene of many of Herakles's labours.

Its forests hide the cercopes, small blue-green monkeys said to descend from two prankster brothers Zeus changed into apes for tormenting Herakles. Each is a magical creature, rare and always met alone, and how they breed is a mystery to the Order; hard to find, they are prized as familiars by Theban magi.

neighbours.name: Mount Pagus
neighbours.summary:
A small mountain south of Smyrna, looking over the city and its bay, crowned by a ruined citadel whose walls and towers have crumbled to a shell. Alexandria only cleared the inside and built wooden houses for its staff, leaving the walls unmended so as not to draw soldiers' eyes. The citadel has a Magic aura of 1, and inside it lie two regiones, one within the other: the ghosts' tent camp (Magic 3) and, at its centre, the covenant's stone houses (Magic 5).

A small Nicene garrison now holds the citadel, put there by the emperor to guard Smyrna against the Turks. The soldiers live in Alexandria's wooden houses, have turned out its covenfolk, and do not know that a regio lies inside the walls, which makes coming and going hard for the Redcaps.

levels.name: The Camp of the Ghosts
levels.notes: A grid of plain cloth tents like the bivouac of Alexander's army, where most of the covenant's ghosts dwell, and Fides, its patron, among them.

levels.name: The Stone Houses of Alexandria
levels.notes: At the heart of the tent camp: the fine stone buildings of the covenant, the old Redcaps' homes, the Tribunal's records and two Hermetic laboratories (one in use); a dozen servants live here.

neighbours.secrets: The glass submarine kept by Alexandria (an iron anima, see the Bestiary) is chained to one of its ships in Smyrna harbour, not here.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Nymphaeum
neighbours.summary:
An imperial palace ten miles south of Smyrna, built some forty years ago by Andronikos I Komnenos and now the residence Theodore Laskaris likes and uses best. The way to it runs through Smyrna's old agora, the oldest and most ruined quarter of the city.

Lone travellers there are sometimes accosted by an old man who says he is Homer: he trails after them asking how his poems are faring and whether they would like a recitation, and runs off if threatened or if a crowd comes near. Some magi take him for a faerie playing Homer, who loved the banks of the nearby Meles; a few Jerbiton think he is the poet himself, made a magic human by becoming a legendary artist.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
neighbours.summary:
Once among the greatest temples of the ancient world, built over a spring sacred to Cybele, the old Earth Mother; an arsonist burned it, and the Ephesians even refused Alexander's offer to rebuild. They went on making and selling images of Diana until St Paul, defied by the craftsmen, prayed and the goddess's stone statue burst into rubble, at which they converted.

The shell stands on a hillside outside the city, most of its stone carried off for building, with a Faerie aura of 2; the statue's broken, mossy head lies in a corner. Stepping over it on the eve of Diana's festival leads into a Faerie regio of aura 4 where the temple stands whole. A faerie calling herself Diana lives there with her faerie deer as servants and invites visitors to hunt stags in the regio's forest. Women who hunt well get small prizes; men she lures by bathing in woodland pools, and any who look on her naked she attacks, setting her stags on them.

levels.name: Diana's Temple
levels.enter: Step over the statue's broken head on the eve of Diana's festival, 13 August
levels.notes: The temple whole and splendid, with a forest round it where the faerie Diana hunts stags with her herd of faerie deer.

neighbours.name: The Cave of the Seven Sleepers
neighbours.summary:
A cave a few leagues outside Ephesus, a great pilgrimage site. In Decius's persecution seven Christians fled into it with Roman soldiers behind them and were sealed in; they lay down to sleep, and woke when an earthquake broke the seal, to find more than a century gone and the empire Christian. They lived long and were buried in the cave. The Qur'an tells the story too, oddly with a dog among them.

The cave has a Divine aura of 3, which has replaced the Magic aura it once had; the old regio survives, hard to enter, with a Magic aura of 6 and dilated time. Alexandria's Redcaps think vis might be gathered there, but the gatherer would have to stay the night, with no knowing how long would pass outside.

levels.name: The Sleepers' Regio
levels.notes: The old Magic regio, hard to enter but still there; time is dilated inside.

neighbours.name: Thrakesion
neighbours.summary: Nicaea's southernmost theme, Thrakesion, running from Lydia to the Maeander and its fertile basin: the old Ionia and Caria, once thick with towns and ports along the Aegean. Centuries of war with the Turks have drawn its people into walled cities, Philadelphia the chief. The Maeander has been Nicaea's southern frontier since 1211, when Theodore Laskaris beat Kaykhusraw I of Rum at Antioch-on-the-Maeander.

neighbours.name: The Maeander
neighbours.summary:
The longest river of Asia Minor, winding from the interior to the Aegean: fast and deep, if not always wide, so only small sailing or rowing craft can use it.

One small tributary, of great interest to Redcaps, flows into a cave, and a boat that follows it through comes out on the Alfeios in Elis, on the western Peloponnese: an hour's sail for a journey of days across the Aegean. The underground river is magical in ways Hermetic theory cannot explain, and Redcaps just call it a natural Mercere Portal. Alexandria's glass submarine cannot use it, the Maeander being too muddy and narrow.

neighbours.name: The Vineyard of Dionysus on Mount Tmolus
neighbours.summary:
Of the many vineyards on the slopes of Mount Tmolus above Philadelphia, one has borne grapes for centuries, and its wine is unusually strong, above all for women. Hermetic inquiry shows it was once a festival ground of Dionysus, where satyrs and maenads (women driven to frenzy by wine) gathered. It has a Faerie aura of 3.

No magus has found a satyr, though tales of them are many; the women of Philadelphia know that if enough of them get drunk and dance wildly, the satyrs come.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: its grapes can be distilled into Mentem vis, 1 pawn for each hundred gallons of wine. The book names no one who gathers it.

neighbours.name: The Field of Antioch-on-the-Maeander
neighbours.summary:
The battlefield of 1211 where Nicaea's southern border was won. French and Greek chronicles agree the Turks were winning until Theodore Laskaris met Sultan Kaykhusraw himself; the sultan, on an enormous horse, struck the emperor down but was killed before he could finish him. The French say Laskaris did the killing; the Greeks tell of a strange French knight who came from nowhere and slew the sultan. That blow saved the empire and stilled the Turkish threat for years.

The Tribunal whispers that the knight was a magus in disguise, which would be a gross breach of the Code. The field, at the far frontier, is not easy to reach. A senior magus may ask player magi to find out before the Tribunal of 1221.
neighbours.secrets: The magus who sets them on may suspect someone and want proof, or may be the knight himself, testing how easily the truth can be found.

neighbours.name: Mount Sipylus
neighbours.summary:
A dead volcano some 5000 feet high near the Maeander's headwaters, seen from Smyrna and the coast, with a crater lake at its summit. Legend makes it the seat of Tantalus, son of Zeus, whose royal city on the peak was destroyed when he betrayed his father; his treasury is said to lie sunk under the lake's murky bed.

Each version of his crime hints at lost lore. Diodorus says he told secrets learned from Zeus, which stirs Bonisagus who would break the Limits of magic; Pindar says he stole nectar and ambrosia, and Epidauros's magi wonder whether these could better a Longevity Ritual; a third tale, dear to Verditius, has him keep a golden automaton that guarded Zeus's temple on Crete. No seeker has yet found the treasury or any of its marvels.

neighbours.name: Paphlagonia and Pontus
neighbours.summary:
The southern shore of the Black Sea east of Bithynia: Paphlagonia in the west, Pontus in the east, both mountainous with only a thin strip of farmed and settled coast under thick broadleaf forest, mild in winter and muggy in summer. The Pontic mountains close it to the south, wooded and snowy most of the year, and the rivers cutting down through them make valleys rich in hazelnuts, plums, cherries and pears.

The Komnenos brothers, Alexios and David, took both provinces soon after Constantinople fell, but in 1220 three powers share the coast: Nicaea as far as Amastris, midway along Paphlagonia; the Seljuks from Sinope, where Paphlagonia meets Pontus; and Trebizond in the far half of Pontus. The last real fighting was in 1214, when Theodore Laskaris took Amastris, and all has been quiet since. Merchants of all three meet to trade, all three great cities have Genoese and Venetian trade agreements, and foreigners pay only a tax on what they bring in.

neighbours.name: The Gardens of Trebizond
neighbours.summary:
Trebizond's beauty has given rise to several Magic auras, most of them in the city's gardens and arboretums (the book gives no strengths). Magic has soaked into the plants, and the city has many magical herbs, fruits and hardwoods: one grove's bark is as hard as iron and must soak in water a year before it can be worked, and Aristotle wrote of some of them, among them a vine dripping honey that cures madmen and epileptics.

Lately bardi have plagued the city: shapeshifting spirits in the form of a she-jackal, solitary, whose wail foretells a death. The clergy call them demons, the townsfolk faeries; no magus has caught one to study. Their warnings are uncannily true: everyone who has seen the jackal and heard it wail has soon lost someone dear.
neighbours.secrets:
Fishermen of the docks have lately seen a huge, savage shark off the shore that has killed several men who tried to kill it, and they are sure it hunts the Pearl of Peroz, which must be somewhere in the city. That pearl, the greatest ever seen, hung from the ear of King Peroz of Persia, who marched into eastern Anatolia against the Ephthalite Huns in the fifth century. A fisherman found it by watching a monstrous shark follow an oyster that showed it its pearl; he threw the oyster ashore and was eaten, and the shark haunted the king whenever he went near the sea.
